lessons.title: Ich werde es schaffen: Futur I, the B1 step
lessons.goal: Use werden plus an infinitive for promises, predictions and decisions, also at the end of a side clause: Ich werde dich besuchen. Ich glaube, dass es klappen wird.

grammar.point: Futur I is werden in position 2 plus an infinitive at the end: Ich werde dir helfen. It is used for promises, predictions and clear decisions. In a dass-clause werden stands last, after the infinitive: …, dass ich dich besuchen werde. For a fixed date the present is often better (Im März fahre ich nach Wien). Futur (it will happen) is not würde (only a wish).
grammar.oneLine: Ich verspreche dir, dass ich dich besuchen werde.

mistake.wrong: Ich verspreche, dass ich werde dich besuchen.
mistake.right: Ich verspreche, dass ich dich besuchen werde.
mistake.why: In a side clause werden is the finite verb, so it goes to the very end, after the infinitive.

terms.meaning: the future form: werden plus an infinitive
a statement about what you think will happen

cards.title: Before we start: from 'Am Wochenende werde ich …' to 'Ich verspreche dir, dass ich dich besuchen werde'
cards.body: This chapter is called Blick nach vorn: a look ahead. It is the end of December, and the WG sits at the table with plans for the new year. You already know werden plus an infinitive for a plan. Today werden gets bigger jobs: a promise, a prediction, and a place at the very end of a side clause.
steps: You already know: Am Wochenende werde ich eine Radtour machen. werden plus an infinitive says what you will do.
New today: Ich werde dich jeden Monat besuchen. and Du wirst es schaffen!: a promise and a prediction.
By the end you can: use Futur I for promises and predictions, put werden last in a dass-clause, and tell Futur from würde.

examples.de: Am Wochenende werde ich eine Radtour machen.
examples.en: At the weekend I will go on a bike tour.
examples.why: You know this: a plan with werden.

examples.de: Ich werde dich jeden Monat besuchen.
examples.en: I will visit you every month.
examples.why: New today: the same pattern now carries a promise.

cards.more: Think of werden as a little flag on the second seat of the sentence. The flag says: this is about later. The real action word waits at the far end, like a passenger who has not arrived yet. You already planted this flag for weekend plans. Today you plant it for bigger things: a promise to a friend, a guess about the weather, and a flag that sits last inside a side clause.

cards.title: Plans at the WG table
cards.body: Look for werden in position 2 and a second verb at the very end: werde … arbeiten, werde … besuchen. That is Futur I, the future with werden. You know it from A2. Mira uses the present instead because her date is fixed: Im Sommer bin ich fertig. Both ways are normal German.
cards.lead: A scene from the WG kitchen at the end of December. Read it once and find werden plus a second verb at the end of each line. The next cards take the pattern apart.

examples.de: Ich werde ab März ein Jahr in Wien arbeiten.
examples.en: From March I will work for a year in Wien.

examples.de: Ich werde dich jeden Monat besuchen.
examples.en: I will visit you every month.

examples.de: Ich werde im Januar einen Kochkurs machen.
examples.en: In January I will do a cooking course.

deeper.text: Ab works like an arrival sign: it marks the day something starts. Ab März, ab Montag, ab nächster Woche. It takes the dative, so after an adjective you hear the -er and -em endings: ab nächstem Monat, ab nächster Woche. Bis marks the end, ab marks the start.

example.de: Ab nächstem Monat wohne ich allein.
example.en: From next month I will live alone.

cards.more: Picture the kitchen table like a stage. Each person says one line, and every line has the same shape: I, then werde, then the details, then the verb at the end. Anna's line is the longest, but the shape stays the same. Mira steps out of the pattern and says bin instead of werde. That is allowed when the date is certain, because the time word already points to the future.
steps: Anna: Ich werde ab März ein Jahr in Wien arbeiten.
Ben: Dann werde ich dich jeden Monat besuchen.
Mira: Im Sommer bin ich mit dem Bachelor fertig.
Leon: Ich werde im Januar einen Kochkurs machen.
Mira: Und was sagt das Atelier in Wien, Anna?
Anna: Es hat mir eine Stelle angeboten. Ich freue mich schon!
Ben: Dann ist das neue Jahr bei uns ein ganz neuer Start.

cards.title: The forms of werden
cards.body: werden is irregular. Learn it as a set: ich werde, du wirst, er wird, wir werden, ihr werdet, sie werden. After the finite form the second verb is an infinitive at the very end. Notice that wirst and wird have no d.
cards.lead: Now the engine of the whole lesson: werden in all persons. Learn this table once, because every Futur sentence in this chapter uses one of these six forms.

examples.de: Du wirst es bestimmt schaffen.
examples.en: You will definitely manage it.

examples.de: Anna wird viel malen.
examples.en: Anna will paint a lot.

examples.de: Wir werden uns jede Woche anrufen.
examples.en: We will call each other every week.

examples.de: Ihr werdet Spaß haben.
examples.en: You (all) will have fun.

deeper.text: Look at du wirst and er wird: the stem werd- loses its d. Nobody says werdst or werdt. This happens with only a few verbs, and werden is the most important one. The same shortening gives you the very useful sentence Ich werde dich vermissen, which people say when a friend moves away.

example.de: Ich werde dich vermissen.
example.en: I will miss you.

cards.more: Imagine werden as a chameleon that changes with the person. With ich it ends in -e, with wir and sie in -en, with ihr in -et. Only du and er/sie/es drop the d and become wirst and wird. That is the whole trick. The second verb does not change at all: it always stays as the plain infinitive, waiting at the end of the sentence like a suitcase by the door.
steps: 1  Take the right form of werden for your subject.
2  Put it in position 2.
3  Put the infinitive at the very end.

cards.title: Three jobs of Futur I
cards.body: Futur I does three jobs: a promise (Ich werde dir helfen.), a prediction (Es wird regnen.), and a clear decision about yourself (Ich werde einen Kochkurs machen.). The pattern is always the same, only your reason for saying it changes.
cards.lead: You know how to build Futur. Now you see what people actually do with it: promise, predict and decide. Each job has its own short example sentence you can reuse.

examples.de: Ich werde dir beim Umzug helfen.
examples.en: I will help you with the move.
examples.why: A promise.

examples.de: Morgen wird es kalt und windig sein.
examples.en: Tomorrow it will be cold and windy.
examples.why: A prediction.

examples.de: Du wirst im Sommer die Prüfung bestehen.
examples.en: You will pass the exam in summer.
examples.why: A prediction with a personal feeling.

deeper.text: For a fixed calendar plan Germans often prefer the present: Im März fahre ich nach Wien. Futur adds weight. It sounds like a promise or a decision you want others to hear. So with a date, choose the present. For a promise or a prediction, choose werden.

example.de: Im März fahre ich nach Wien.
example.en: In March I am going to Wien.

cards.more: Imagine three little speech bubbles. The first one is a hand shake: Ich werde dir helfen, a promise. The second is a crystal ball: Es wird regnen, a prediction. The third is a thick line under your own name: Ich werde einen Kochkurs machen, a decision. The sentence looks the same in all three bubbles. What changes is what you want the other person to feel: trust, expectation, or my mind is made up.
steps: 1  Ask: do I give my word, guess the future, or decide?
2  The same pattern fits all three: werden at position 2, infinitive at the end.

cards.title: werden at the end of a side clause
cards.body: In a dass-clause the finite verb goes to the very end, and that is werden. The infinitive comes right before it: …, dass ich dich besuchen werde. The order is infinitive, then werde, wirst or wird. Nothing may stand behind werden.
cards.lead: So far werden stood in position 2. In a side clause it moves to the very end. This card shows the new order with three of the WG's own sentences.

examples.de: Ich verspreche dir, dass ich dich besuchen werde.
examples.en: I promise you that I will visit you.

examples.de: Ich glaube, dass es klappen wird.
examples.en: I believe that it will work out.

examples.de: Mira sagt, dass sie im Sommer fertig sein wird.
examples.en: Mira says that she will be finished in summer.

deeper.text: With a separable verb the infinitive stays in one piece and still comes before werden: Ich verspreche, dass ich früh aufstehen werde. The prefix does not jump to the end of the clause the way it does in a main clause. Whole verb first, then werde. This is one place where Futur is easier than the present.

example.de: Ich verspreche, dass ich früh aufstehen werde.
example.en: I promise that I will get up early.

cards.more: A side clause is a box, and the box closes with its finite verb. In a dass-box the closing piece is werde, wirst or wird. The infinitive sits just in front of it, like a dog beside its owner. So you write the whole story first, then the infinitive, then werden to close the lid. You cannot put anything behind it. If you hear a sentence end on wird or werde, you are probably in a Futur side clause.
steps: 1  Start with the main clause and a comma: Ich verspreche dir,
2  Add dass, the subject, and the details.
3  End with the infinitive, then werde / wirst / wird.

cards.title: Futur or würde?
cards.body: Futur says it will really happen: Anna wird nach Wien gehen. Konjunktiv II with würde says it is only a wish or an if-idea: Ben würde auch gern nach Wien gehen. Sure about it: werden. Only dreaming: würde. You know würde from B1 chapter 4.
cards.lead: Two forms look almost the same, werden and würde, and they mean different things. This card puts them side by side, so you hear the difference between a decision and a dream.

examples.de: Anna wird nach Wien gehen.
examples.en: Anna will go to Wien.
examples.why: Decided: it will happen.

examples.de: Ben würde auch gern nach Wien gehen.
examples.en: Ben would like to go to Wien too.
examples.why: A wish: it will not happen.

examples.de: Leon würde gern jeden Tag kochen.
examples.en: Leon would like to cook every day.
examples.why: A dream, not a plan.

deeper.text: Futur can also be a strict order: Du wirst jetzt sofort aufräumen! It sounds like a parent with a clear plan. For a polite request use würde: Würdest du bitte aufräumen? Learners often mix these up, because English will sounds polite in Will you help me? In German that is würde, not wirst.

example.de: Würdest du bitte kurz helfen?
example.en: Would you please help for a moment?

cards.more: Think of two roads. Werden is the road you are already driving on: it leads to Wien, and you will arrive. Würde is a road on the map that you only look at with your finger and say: it would be nice. The words are neighbours, one letter apart in the middle, but the roads are different. Ask yourself: is this decided, or only imagined? Decided means werden, imagined means würde.

rows: only a wish or an idea
Ich würde gern nach Wien gehen.

steps: 1  Is it decided or very likely? Use werden.
2  Is it only a wish or what if? Use würde.

cards.title: werden: will or become?
cards.body: werden has two meanings. Alone it means become: Ich werde müde. With an infinitive it means will: Ich werde schlafen. Both together are possible: Es wird kalt werden, it will become cold. Look at the end of the sentence to decide.
cards.lead: You met werden = become in A2, and now werden = will. This card helps you tell them apart in one glance, so you never read a Futur sentence the wrong way.

examples.de: Ich werde müde.
examples.en: I am getting tired.
examples.why: werden = become: no infinitive.

examples.de: Ich werde früh schlafen.
examples.en: I will sleep early.
examples.why: werden = will: infinitive at the end.

examples.de: Es wird im Winter kalt werden.
examples.en: It will become cold in winter.
examples.why: Both: will + become.

deeper.text: Es wird kalt werden is correct, but many speakers say only Es wird kalt, and the present already carries the future. Listen for this in weather forecasts: Morgen wird es kälter. German likes the short version when the time word, like morgen, is clear. Use the long one when you want to sound careful.

example.de: Morgen wird es kälter.
example.en: Tomorrow it will be colder.

cards.more: Imagine a coin with two faces. On one face werden means to become: you look at the word after it and see an adjective or a noun, like müde or Lehrerin. On the other face werden means will: you look at the end of the sentence and see an infinitive, like schlafen. When both appear, the sentence has two faces at once and you read it as will become. Always check the word at the end.
steps: 1  Adjective or noun after werden? It means become.
2  Infinitive at the end? It means will.
3  Both? It means will become.

Ich glaube, dass wird es klappen.

drills.explanation: Ich glaube, dass es klappen wird.

drills.hint: A dream, not a decision: use the form from B1 chapter 4.

Jeden Monat werde ich dich besuchen.
blind.hint: Ich + werde + dich + time + infinitive at the end.
blind.explanation: Ich werde dich jeden Monat besuchen.

Morgen wird es kalt und windig sein. Anna wird sicher viel malen.
Ich werde im Januar einen Kochkurs machen. Im März fahre ich nach Wien.

lessons.title: Er wird wohl im Stau stehen: guesses and other ways to talk about the future
lessons.goal: Guess about the present with wird wohl, and choose the best way to talk about the future: present, werden, möchte, vorhaben or sich vornehmen plus zu.

grammar.topic: Futur for guesses; other ways to talk about the future
grammar.point: Futur I with wohl, sicher or wahrscheinlich is a guess about now: Er wird wohl noch arbeiten. Wird schon comforts: Das wird schon! Other ways to speak of the future are the present with a time word (Im Januar fange ich an), möchte, vorhaben or beschließen plus zu, and sich vornehmen plus zu. anfangen and aufhören also take zu plus infinitive. Ich will means I want, not I will.
grammar.oneLine: Er wird wohl noch in der Küche sein.

mistake.right: Ich rufe dich morgen an. / Ich will dich morgen anrufen.
mistake.why: will means want. After a modal verb the infinitive goes to the very end of the sentence.

terms.meaning: werden with wohl, sicher or wahrscheinlich, about something happening at this moment
a decision to do something, often at New Year

cards.title: Before we start: from 'Ich werde …' to 'Er wird wohl noch schlafen'
cards.body: Futur I is not only for promises. People also use it to guess what is going on right now: Where is Leon? He will probably still be in the kitchen. Today you also learn five ways to talk about the future, so you can pick the one that fits.
steps: You already know: Ich habe vor, mehr zu lesen. vorhaben plus zu plus an infinitive says what you plan.
New today: Leon ist nicht da. Er wird wohl noch in der Küche sein. A guess about now, with werden and wohl.
By the end you can: guess with wird wohl, and choose between the present, werden, möchte, vorhaben and sich vornehmen.

examples.de: Ich habe vor, mehr zu lesen.
examples.en: I plan to read more.
examples.why: You know this: a plan with vorhaben.

examples.de: Er wird wohl noch in der Küche sein.
examples.en: He is probably still in the kitchen.
examples.why: New today: werden for a guess about now.

cards.more: Imagine you stand at a window and look for a friend who is late. You cannot see him, so you guess: he is probably still at work. German uses werden for this guess and adds the little word wohl, which means probably. It looks just like a promise, but the clue is the little word and the time: you are guessing about now, not about tomorrow. And you meet a few other ways to speak about the future.

cards.title: Where is Leon?
cards.body: It is eight o'clock and Leon is late. The friends guess where he is: Er wird wohl noch bei Herrn Ali arbeiten. This is Futur I, but the time is now, not later. The little word wohl shows it is only a guess. Er wird schon kommen means: do not worry, he will come.
cards.lead: A short scene in the WG kitchen. Everyone waits for Leon and guesses. Find werden, the little word wohl or schon, and the infinitive at the end.

examples.de: Er wird wohl noch bei Herrn Ali arbeiten.
examples.en: He is probably still working at Herr Ali's.

examples.de: Der Bus wird wohl im Stau stehen.
examples.en: The bus is probably stuck in traffic.

examples.de: Er wird schon kommen.
examples.en: He will come, do not worry.

deeper.text: The present works for a guess too: Er ist wohl noch bei Herrn Ali. The meaning is the same. The Futur version sounds a little more careful and a bit more spoken in everyday talk. If you only remember wohl, you can already guess correctly. But then you also understand Futur guesses when you hear them.

example.de: Er ist wohl noch bei Herrn Ali.
example.en: He is probably still at Herr Ali's.

cards.more: Think of a detective at the window. He has no proof, only clues: Saturday, Herr Ali's restaurant, eight o'clock. So he says: Er wird wohl noch arbeiten. The word wohl is like a little question mark that goes inside the sentence. Without wohl, a hearer would think you are talking about the future. With wohl, they know you are guessing about the present moment, right now.
steps: Mira: Es ist schon acht Uhr. Wo ist Leon?
Ben: Heute ist Samstag. Er wird wohl noch bei Herrn Ali arbeiten.
Anna: Oder der Bus wird wohl im Stau stehen.
Mira: Er hat nicht angerufen. Ich mache mir Sorgen.
Ben: Keine Angst, er wird schon kommen.
Leon: Entschuldigung! Der Bus hat im Stau gestanden.

cards.title: Futur for a guess about now
cards.body: For a guess about now use werden plus wohl, sicher or wahrscheinlich, and an infinitive at the end. The time is the present moment: Anna wird sicher noch im Atelier sein. The word wird schon is different: it calms someone down about the future.
cards.lead: You have seen the guess pattern in a story. Here it is as a rule you can reuse: werden plus a little word that says how sure you are.

examples.de: Frau Weber wird wohl schon schlafen.
examples.en: Frau Weber is probably asleep already.

examples.de: Anna wird sicher noch im Atelier sein.
examples.en: Anna is surely still in the studio.

examples.de: Mira wird wahrscheinlich müde sein.
examples.en: Mira is probably tired.

deeper.text: Wird schon is one of the most common phrases in everyday German. Das wird schon! means: it will be fine. You say it to a friend who is nervous about an exam. It works without any other word, and everyone understands it as comfort, not as a guess. It is a great chunk to learn as a whole.

example.de: Keine Angst, das wird schon!
example.en: Do not worry, it will be fine!

cards.more: A guess has three little helpers. Wohl says: maybe, probably. Sicher says: I am quite sure. Wahrscheinlich says: very likely. You pick one helper, put it behind werden, and the sentence becomes a guess about now. And the word schon is different: when you hear wird schon, it is a pat on the shoulder, not a guess. It says: it will be okay, wait and see.
steps: 1  Pick a helper word: wohl, sicher, wahrscheinlich.
2  werden in position 2, helper word in the middle.
3  Infinitive at the end.

cards.title: Five ways to say future
cards.body: German has five common ways to talk about the future. The present with a time word, werden, wollen or möchten, vorhaben, planen or beschließen with zu, and sich vornehmen with zu. Each gives a different shade: fixed, promised, wished, planned, or resolved.
cards.lead: You now know werden. This card puts it next to the other four ways to talk about the future, so you see which shade each one carries.

examples.de: Im Januar fange ich an.
examples.en: In January I start.
examples.why: Present + time word.

examples.de: Ich möchte mehr Sport machen.
examples.en: I would like to do more sport.
examples.why: möchten: a wish.

examples.de: Ben hat vor, im Juli fertig zu werden.
examples.en: Ben plans to be finished in July.
examples.why: vorhaben + zu: a plan.

deeper.text: Careful with will. In German ich will means I want, not I will. Ich will einen Kaffee is a clear wish and can sound strong. For a promise use werden. For a polite wish use möchte. This is the classic false friend between English and German, and it can make you sound much more demanding than you mean.

example.de: Ich will Koch werden.
example.en: I want to become a cook.

cards.more: Imagine a rack of five tools. The first, present plus a time word, is a calendar: Im Januar fange ich an. The second, werden, is a handshake. The third, möchte or will, is a wish list. The fourth, vorhaben, is a plan in your notebook. The fifth, sich vornehmen, is a note on your fridge for the new year. They all point to later, but each one feels different. You choose the tool that fits what you want to say.

rows: Ich habe vor, mehr zu lesen.
Ich nehme mir vor, mehr zu lesen.

steps: 1  Is there a fixed date? Present + time word.
2  Promise or forecast? werden.
3  Wish? möchte. Plan? vorhaben. Resolution? sich vornehmen.

cards.title: Gute Vorsätze zu Silvester
cards.body: At Silvester, on 31 December, many people in Deutschland, Österreich and the Schweiz make gute Vorsätze, resolutions for the new year. Before midnight they say Guten Rutsch! To say what you resolve, use sich vornehmen plus zu: Ich nehme mir vor, jeden Tag zu laufen.
cards.lead: It is Silvester, the last night of the year. Here is the German way to talk about resolutions and to wish a happy start. Look for vornehmen and zu.

examples.de: Ich nehme mir vor, jeden Tag zu laufen.
examples.en: I resolve to run every day.

examples.de: Anna nimmt sich vor, jeden Tag zu malen.
examples.en: Anna resolves to paint every day.

examples.de: Zu Silvester fassen viele Leute gute Vorsätze.
examples.en: At Silvester many people make good resolutions.

deeper.text: People explain Guten Rutsch in two ways. One says it comes from rutschen, to slide into the new year. The other links it to a Hebrew word for the head of the year. Nobody knows for sure. You wish it before the new year starts, not after 1 January. Afterwards you say Frohes neues Jahr!

example.de: Guten Rutsch ins neue Jahr!
example.en: A good slide into the new year!

cards.more: Imagine writing a note to yourself on a mirror. Ich nehme mir vor means: I take for myself, I put it on my list. Then comes the thing you want to do, with zu and an infinitive at the end. The word mir stays small, but it is important: it says this is a promise to me, not to someone else. At Silvester everyone has such a note, and the phrase Guten Rutsch is the sparkling wine toast over it.
steps: 1  Ich nehme mir vor, …
2  Add what you want to do.
3  Put zu directly before the infinitive: … jeden Tag zu laufen.

cards.title: anfangen and aufhören with zu
cards.body: After anfangen, aufhören and beginnen you use zu plus an infinitive at the end of the clause, set off by a comma: Leon fängt im Januar an, einen Kochkurs zu besuchen. The separable prefix an or auf stays before the comma.
cards.lead: Two more verbs take zu plus an infinitive, like vorhaben: anfangen for the start, aufhören for the end. Look at where an and auf go, and where zu goes.

examples.de: Leon fängt im Januar an, einen Kochkurs zu besuchen.
examples.en: Leon starts to take a cooking course in January.

examples.de: Mira hört auf, so viel Kaffee zu trinken.
examples.en: Mira stops drinking so much coffee.

examples.de: Anna fängt im März an, in Wien zu arbeiten.
examples.en: Anna starts to work in Wien in March.

deeper.text: When the infinitive itself is separable, zu moves inside the verb and everything is written as one word: Ich fange an, früh aufzustehen. Not zu aufstehen. This small rule is common with verbs like aufstehen, anrufen, einkaufen. You will meet it again and again, so learn it with one good example.

example.de: Ich fange an, früh aufzustehen.
example.en: I start to get up early.

cards.more: Think of two doors. Anfangen opens a door: something starts. Aufhören closes a door: something stops. Both ask for a second action, and that action always comes with zu in front of it, like a little key. The key goes right before the infinitive at the end. If the infinitive has a prefix, the key sits inside the word: aufzustehen. The comma before the new part is like a fence between the two pieces.

rows: Mira hört auf, Kaffee zu trinken.
Anna beginnt, in Wien zu arbeiten.

steps: 1  Main clause with anfangen or aufhören, comma.
2  Add the details of the second action.
3  zu directly before the infinitive (inside it if it is separable).

cards.title: Which form fits?
cards.body: Choose by asking one question. Is the date fixed? Use the present. Do you promise or predict? Use werden. Do you wish? Use möchte or will. Do you plan or resolve? Use vorhaben or sich vornehmen plus zu. One thought can often fit two forms, but this helps you choose.
cards.lead: You know five ways to talk about the future. This last card gives you a short decision list, so you can choose the right form in a real conversation.

examples.de: Im Januar beginnt der Kurs.
examples.en: The course begins in January.
examples.why: A fixed date: present.

examples.de: Ich verspreche dir: Ich werde anrufen.
examples.en: I promise you: I will call.
examples.why: A promise: werden.

examples.de: Ich nehme mir vor, weniger Kaffee zu trinken.
examples.en: I resolve to drink less coffee.
examples.why: A resolution: sich vornehmen.

deeper.text: In letters and official texts you also find beabsichtigen: Wir beabsichtigen, im Mai umzuziehen. It means to intend, and it sounds formal. In daily talk you hear vorhaben or planen instead. Both sentences say nearly the same thing, but beabsichtigen belongs in a letter to an office, not in a talk with a friend.

example.de: Wir beabsichtigen, im Mai umzuziehen.
example.en: We intend to move in May.

cards.more: Picture a small traffic light for your sentence. Green: the date is fixed, so you simply say the present with a time word. Yellow: you promise or predict, so you add werden. Blue: you wish something, so you use möchte. Purple: you plan, so you use vorhaben. White: you resolve, so you use sich vornehmen. You do not need to learn all five at once. Start with the question: how sure am I, and how big is my wish?

rows: Ich habe vor, mehr zu lesen.
Ich nehme mir vor, mehr zu lesen.

steps: 1  Fixed date? Present.
2  Promise or forecast? werden.
3  Wish? möchte. Plan? vorhaben. Resolution? sich vornehmen.

lessons.title: Gute Ratschläge für das neue Jahr
lessons.goal: Understand advice and warnings, read an advice column and react politely: Ich rate dir, früh anzufangen. Es lohnt sich, … zu …. Ich überlege es mir.

grammar.point: Advice patterns with zu plus infinitive: Ich rate dir, … zu …, Es lohnt sich, … zu …, Vergiss nicht, … zu …. With dass and the verb last: Pass auf, dass …. warnen takes vor plus the dative: Ich warne dich vor dem Stress. After raten you never use dass plus zu together. React with Danke, das ist ein guter Tipp. / Das werde ich machen. / Ich überlege es mir.

mistake.wrong: Ich rate dir, dass du früh anzufangen.
mistake.why: With zu plus infinitive there is no dass and no du. dass belongs to a clause with a subject, zu to the infinitive alone.

terms.meaning: a newspaper column where an expert answers readers' questions
a sentence that tells someone to be careful

cards.title: Before we start: from 'Du solltest …' to 'Es lohnt sich, …'
cards.body: Before a big change, everyone gives advice. You already know Du solltest … and An deiner Stelle würde ich …. Today you learn more ways to hear and give advice, and how to answer it. There is no new grammar in this lesson, only new patterns made from words you know.
steps: You already know: Du solltest früher ins Bett gehen. and An deiner Stelle würde ich anfangen.
New today: Ich rate dir, früh anzufangen. and Es lohnt sich, eine Liste zu schreiben.
By the end you can: understand advice and warnings, read an advice column, and react in a polite way.

examples.de: Du solltest früher ins Bett gehen.
examples.en: You should go to bed earlier.
examples.why: You know this: advice with sollte.

examples.de: Ich rate dir, früh anzufangen.
examples.en: I advise you to start early.
examples.why: New today: advice with raten plus zu.

cards.more: Imagine a friend who is about to move. Everyone around her has a tip. One person says it softly, one says it clearly, and one gives a warning. This lesson is about those voices. You will hear them in the kitchen, read them in a newspaper column, and answer them with short, polite phrases. You do not need new grammar, only the patterns that carry the advice.

cards.title: Advice in the kitchen
cards.body: Frau Weber and Herr Ali give advice. Frau Weber says Ich rate dir, … zu …, and Herr Ali says Pass auf, dass …. Another common pattern is Vergiss nicht, … zu …. After raten and vergessen the second verb comes with zu at the end.
cards.lead: The WG kitchen again. Frau Weber advises Anna, and Herr Ali advises Leon. Find the advice sentences and look at where the verb and the little word zu stand.

examples.de: Ich rate dir, schon jetzt eine Wohnung zu suchen.
examples.en: I advise you to look for a flat already now.

examples.de: Pass auf, dass du nicht zu viel arbeitest.
examples.en: Take care that you do not work too much.

examples.de: Vergiss nicht, mir eine Postkarte zu schicken!
examples.en: Do not forget to send me a postcard!

deeper.text: Aufpassen is separable, so in the imperative the prefix goes to the end: Pass auf! With a side clause you add dass: Pass auf, dass du nicht zu viel arbeitest. A friend says Pass auf dich auf! when you leave, and it means take care of yourself. It is a very warm goodbye between friends.

example.de: Pass auf dich auf!
example.en: Take care of yourself!

cards.more: Think of advice as a little gift with a label. Ich rate dir is a gift with a label: I advise you. Pass auf, dass is a gift with a sign: watch out that. Vergiss nicht is a gift with a string around your finger: do not forget. In each of them, the advice itself comes after the label. If it is a zu-piece, the little word zu sits right before the verb at the end. If it is a dass-piece, the verb is last.
steps: Frau Weber: Anna, ich rate dir, schon jetzt eine Wohnung in Wien zu suchen.
Anna: Das ist ein guter Tipp, Frau Weber.
Frau Weber: Und vergiss nicht, mir eine Postkarte zu schicken!
Herr Ali: Leon, pass auf, dass du nicht zu viel arbeitest.
Leon: Keine Sorge, Herr Ali. Der Kochkurs ist nur am Donnerstag.
Herr Ali: Gut. Dann wirst du am Samstag noch Kraft haben.

cards.title: Advice patterns
cards.body: Here are the main advice patterns of this lesson: Ich rate dir, … zu …, Es lohnt sich, … zu …, Pass auf, dass …, Vergiss nicht, … zu …, Am besten …, Du müsstest mal …. Learn them as small frames and fill in your own verb.
cards.lead: You met the patterns in a conversation. Here they are in one table, so you can reuse them like a toolbox the next time you give a tip.

examples.de: Es lohnt sich, eine Liste zu schreiben.
examples.en: It is worth writing a list.

examples.de: Am besten fängst du heute an.
examples.en: It is best if you start today.

examples.de: Du müsstest mal früher ins Bett gehen.
examples.en: You should go to bed earlier for once.

deeper.text: Es lohnt sich is always used with es and sich: it is a fixed pair. You cannot leave out sich. The negative is common in everyday talk: Das lohnt sich nicht! means it is not worth it. You can also say Es lohnt sich für mich. Remember the two small words, es and sich, because learners often forget them.

example.de: Das lohnt sich nicht!
example.en: That is not worth it!

cards.more: Imagine a toolbox with six tools. Each tool has the same shape on the outside, but a different job on the inside. Ich rate dir is a polite push. Es lohnt sich is a reason: it pays off. Pass auf is a warning hand. Vergiss nicht is a reminder. Am besten is the best path. Du müsstest mal is a gentle hint. You choose the tool for the mood you want, and then add your own verb at the end.

rows: Es lohnt sich, eine Liste zu schreiben.
Pass auf, dass du nicht zu müde wirst.
Am besten fängst du heute an.

steps: 1  Pick the frame that fits your mood.
2  Fill in your own verb at the end.
3  After zu-frames the verb with zu comes last.

cards.title: Warnings
cards.body: To warn someone, say warnen vor plus the dative: Ich warne dich vor zu viel Stress. Shorter warnings are Vorsicht mit …! and Lieber nicht …. After vor you always use the dative: vor dem Stress, vor der Kälte.
cards.lead: Advice can also be a warning. This card shows three short ways to warn a person, and one case you must remember: warnen vor takes the dative.

examples.de: Ich warne dich vor zu viel Stress.
examples.en: I warn you about too much stress.

examples.de: Frau Weber warnt Anna vor der Kälte in Wien.
examples.en: Frau Weber warns Anna about the cold in Wien.

examples.de: Vorsicht mit dem Messer, Leon!
examples.en: Careful with the knife, Leon!

deeper.text: After vor the dative is needed: vor dem Stress, vor der Kälte, vor dem Regen. Many learners use the accusative here because warnen has an accusative object, dich. Remember that the preposition vor decides: it takes the dative. A short test: ask wovor? and answer with the dative, vor dem Regen.

example.de: Ich warne dich vor dem Stress.
example.en: I warn you about the stress.

cards.more: Imagine a traffic sign with a little red triangle. Warnen vor is that sign in a sentence. First comes the person you warn, with the accusative: dich, Anna. Then comes the word vor, and after it the thing that is dangerous, with the dative: vor dem Regen, vor der Kälte. The two cases live in one sentence, side by side, like two neighbours: dich for the person, dem or der for the danger. Short signs like Vorsicht! need no grammar at all.

rows: Ich warne dich vor dem Stress.

steps: 1  Say who you warn: Ich warne dich …
2  Add vor and the danger in the dative.
3  Or use a short sign: Vorsicht mit …!

cards.title: The advice column
cards.body: A Ratgeberkolumne is a newspaper column where a reader writes a letter and an expert answers. Read the question first, then find the advice patterns in the answer. Here the column is called „Frag Frau Rat“. The answer uses Sie.
cards.lead: Now you read a real-life type of text: an advice column. Look for the patterns from the last cards. The text is short, so read it twice.

examples.de: Ich rate Ihnen, schon jetzt die Sprache zu üben.
examples.en: I advise you to practise the language already now.

examples.de: Es lohnt sich, neue Leute kennenzulernen.
examples.en: It is worth getting to know new people.

examples.de: Vergessen Sie nicht, Ihre Familie anzurufen.
examples.en: Do not forget to call your family.

deeper.text: In an advice column the answer uses Sie, because the expert does not know the reader. So the imperative is Gehen Sie in einen Kurs, not Geh in einen Kurs. The letter begins with Liebe Frau Rat, and the answer with Liebe Leserin. A reader who writes to a column uses a name like Neu in der Fremde.

example.de: Gehen Sie in einen Kurs.
example.en: Go to a course.

cards.more: Think of the column as a conversation on paper. The reader asks, and the expert answers. First you read the question: what is the problem? Then you read the answer and underline only the advice sentences. They all have a frame you know: Ich rate Ihnen, Es lohnt sich, Vergessen Sie nicht. You do not have to understand every word. If you find the frames, you find the tips.
steps: Liebe Frau Rat,
im März fange ich in einem neuen Land eine neue Stelle an. Ich kenne dort niemanden. Was raten Sie mir?
Eine Leserin
Liebe Leserin,

ich rate Ihnen, schon jetzt die Sprache zu üben. Es lohnt sich, neue Leute kennenzulernen: Gehen Sie in einen Kurs oder in einen Verein. Vergessen Sie nicht, Ihre Familie anzurufen. Und geben Sie sich Zeit, dann wird es schon!

cards.title: Reacting to advice
cards.body: You do not have to follow every tip. Use short phrases to react: Danke, das ist ein guter Tipp. says yes. Das werde ich machen. is a promise. Ich überlege es mir. is a polite maybe. Da bin ich nicht sicher. says you doubt it.
cards.lead: People give you advice, and now you must answer. Here are four short reactions, from yes to no. Pick the one that matches what you really think.

examples.de: Danke, das ist ein guter Tipp.
examples.en: Thanks, that is a good tip.

examples.de: Das werde ich machen.
examples.en: I will do that.

examples.de: Ich überlege es mir.
examples.en: I will think about it.

deeper.text: Ich überlege es mir is a polite maybe, and often it means no. It works like Ich weiß nicht so recht. You say it when you do not want to hurt anyone. If you want to say yes with more energy, add gern: Das mache ich gern. If you really want to say no, you say Das ist nichts für mich.

example.de: Ich weiß nicht so recht.
example.en: I am not so sure.

cards.more: Imagine four buttons on a remote control. The green one says: Danke, das ist ein guter Tipp. The blue one is a promise: Das werde ich machen, the Futur you just learned. The yellow one says: Ich überlege es mir, I will think about it, which is a gentle pause. The red one says: Da bin ich nicht sicher, so you stay honest. You do not need to push every button, only the one that fits.

rows: Danke, das ist ein guter Tipp.

steps: 1  Do you like the tip? Danke, das ist ein guter Tipp.
2  Will you do it? Das werde ich machen.
3  Not sure? Ich überlege es mir.

cards.title: Hidden advice
cards.body: Germans often give advice directly: Ich rate dir, … is clear. But some advice is hidden in questions or soft words. Ich an deiner Stelle … is clear advice. Hast du schon mal überlegt, …? is soft advice. Du könntest ja mal … is a gentle hint.
cards.lead: Not every tip sounds like a tip. Some come as questions. This last card helps you notice advice that is hidden, so you do not miss a hint.

examples.de: Ich an deiner Stelle würde früh anfangen.
examples.en: In your place I would start early.

examples.de: Hast du schon mal überlegt, einen Kurs zu machen?
examples.en: Have you ever thought about doing a course?

examples.de: Du könntest ja mal Frau Weber fragen.
examples.en: You could ask Frau Weber for once.

deeper.text: Small words soften advice. Ja and mal make a suggestion gentler: Du könntest ja mal fragen. Doch makes an imperative friendly: Probier doch mal einen Kurs aus! Without these words, the same tip sounds sharp. Listen for them in conversation: they are signs that someone is advising you kindly.

example.de: Probier doch mal einen Kurs aus!
example.en: Why not try a course?

cards.more: Think of advice as volume. Ich rate dir is loud: it is clear and direct. Ich an deiner Stelle is medium: it still says what to do. Hast du schon mal überlegt is quiet: it is a question, but it hides a tip. Du könntest ja mal is the quietest, almost a whisper. Learn to hear the quiet ones too. In German, a question with schon mal usually means: I think you should.
steps: 1  Listen for questions with schon mal.
2  Listen for könntest and ja mal.
3  Treat them as tips, not as plain questions.

drills.prompt: Frau Weber rät Anna, schon jetzt eine Wohnung ___ suchen.
drills.hint: After raten the second verb comes with a little word before it.
drills.explanation: Ich rate dir, eine Wohnung zu suchen.

drills.prompt: Es lohnt ___, eine Liste zu schreiben.
drills.hint: es lohnt always comes with a second small word.
drills.explanation: Es lohnt sich, eine Liste zu schreiben.

drills.prompt: Ich warne dich ___ Stress.
drills.hint: warnen vor takes the dative, and Stress is a der-noun.
drills.explanation: vor dem Stress: dative masculine.

drills.prompt: Put in order: Do not forget to call your family.
drills.hint: The zu-piece with the separable verb comes last.

lessons.title: Der Kollege, den Kollegen: n-declension (1)
lessons.goal: Decline masculine nouns in -e and der Mensch, der Nachbar, der Herr: den Kollegen, dem Kunden, des Menschen.

grammar.point: A group of masculine nouns adds -n or -en in every case except the nominative singular: der Kollege, den Kollegen, dem Kollegen, des Kollegen, die Kollegen. Group one are masculine nouns in -e (Kollege, Kunde, Junge, Löwe, Neffe, Experte) and the three nouns der Mensch, der Nachbar, der Herr (den Herrn, die Herren). Most are people or animals. Feminine forms are normal: die Kollegin, der Kollegin.

mistake.why: n-nouns get -n in every case except the nominative singular. After dem, den or des you must add the -n yourself.

terms.meaning: a group of masculine nouns that add -n or -en in all cases except the nominative singular
the case of the subject, the one who acts: Der Kunde bestellt.

cards.title: Before we start: from 'Herrn Ali' to 'den Kollegen'
cards.body: You have said Herrn Ali since A2, for example Ich danke Herrn Ali. That -n is not a trick for one name. A whole group of masculine nouns works this way. Today you learn the group: den Kollegen, dem Kunden, des Menschen. A regular customer in Herr Ali's restaurant helps us.
steps: You already know: Ich danke Herrn Ali. and Der Kollege ist nett.
New today: the same -n on many nouns: Ich frage den Kollegen. Ich helfe dem Kunden.
By the end you can: add -n or -en to the nouns of group one in the accusative, dative and genitive, and in the plural.

examples.de: Ich danke Herrn Ali.
examples.en: I thank Mr Ali.
examples.why: You know this: Herrn Ali has an -n.

examples.de: Der Kollege ist nett.
examples.en: The colleague is nice.
examples.why: You know this: the nominative has no ending.

examples.de: Ich frage den Kollegen.
examples.en: I ask the colleague.
examples.why: New today: the same -n appears on the noun.

examples.de: Ich helfe dem Kunden.
examples.en: I help the customer.
examples.why: New today: the dative has it, too.

cards.more: Think of the little -n as a name tag. In Der Kollege ist nett the colleague is the star of the sentence, so he wears no tag. In Ich frage den Kollegen he is only being asked, so the tag -n appears. You have seen this tag on Herrn Ali for a long time. Today you learn that many nouns wear it. First look at who does the action, then check the tag.

cards.title: A regular customer in „Zum Löwen“
cards.body: A regular customer comes to Herr Ali's restaurant every week. Leon works there on Saturdays and asks about him. Look at the noun der Kunde: in Ich kenne den Kunden schon lange it grows an -n. Spot the -n each time the customer is not the one acting.
cards.lead: A scene from Herr Ali's restaurant. Read it once and look at every Kunde. When does the word end in -n, and when not? The next cards explain the rule.

examples.de: Ich kenne den Kunden schon lange.
examples.en: I have known the customer for a long time.

examples.de: Der Kunde bestellt immer den Resteteller.
examples.en: The customer always orders the leftovers plate.

examples.de: Ich gebe dem Kunden eine große Portion.
examples.en: I give the customer a big portion.

deeper.text: A restaurant often has a Stammkunde, a customer who comes again and again. The word is built from der Stamm (trunk) and der Kunde, and it keeps the n-declension: ich kenne meinen Stammkunden. For the woman you say die Stammkundin, a normal feminine noun.

example.de: Wir haben einen Stammkunden im Restaurant.
example.en: We have a regular customer in the restaurant.

cards.more: Imagine a camera that follows the customer through the restaurant. When the camera shows him sitting down and ordering, he is the subject: Der Kunde bestellt. When Herr Ali looks at him or hands him a plate, the customer is on the receiving end: den Kunden, dem Kunden. Every time the camera sees him receive something, the noun gets its -n. Watch for the little word in front: den or dem.
steps: Leon: Wer sitzt dort am Fenster?
Herr Ali: Das ist ein Kunde aus der Nachbarschaft. Ich kenne den Kunden schon lange.
Leon: Was bestellt er?
Herr Ali: Der Kunde bestellt immer den Resteteller. Ich gebe dem Kunden gern eine große Portion.

cards.title: The rule: one case without -n
cards.body: Only the nominative singular has no ending: der Kollege. In the accusative, dative and genitive singular the noun adds -n: den Kollegen, dem Kollegen, des Kollegen. In the plural every case ends in -n as well: die Kollegen. After the first case, the noun never changes again.
cards.lead: Card one showed der Kunde turning into den Kunden. Here you see all four cases of one noun in a table, so the rule becomes visible: one case without -n, everything else with it.

examples.de: Der Kollege kommt heute später.
examples.en: The colleague comes later today.

examples.de: Mira fragt den Kollegen.
examples.en: Mira asks the colleague.

examples.de: Ich helfe dem Kollegen bei der Arbeit.
examples.en: I help the colleague with the work.

examples.de: Das ist das Büro des Kollegen.
examples.en: That is the colleague's office.

deeper.text: The feminine form is a normal noun: die Kollegin, die Kollegin, der Kollegin. Only the masculine noun gets -n. So Ich frage die Kollegin has no -n on the noun, while Ich frage den Kollegen has. If you want to speak about a woman, the -n disappears. The change belongs to the masculine word, not to the job.

example.de: Ich helfe der Kollegin.
example.en: I help the female colleague.

cards.more: Imagine the noun has a light switch. In the nominative the switch is off: der Kollege. In every other case the switch is on, and the -n lights up: den, dem, des Kollegen. This is easier than the adjective endings you learned in A2, because once the -n is on, the noun does not change again. It is always Kollegen. Only the little word in front tells you the case: den, dem or des.

cards.title: Which nouns? The group in -e
cards.body: Masculine nouns that end in -e are the biggest group, mostly people and animals. They already have the -e, so only an -n is added: den Kunden, den Jungen, den Löwen. Learn them as a family of six: Kollege, Kunde, Junge, Löwe, Neffe, Experte.
cards.lead: Card two showed one noun in all cases. Which other nouns behave like der Kollege? The biggest family is the masculine nouns that already end in -e. Here are six of them.

examples.de: Ich kenne den Jungen aus dem Haus.
examples.en: I know the boy from the house.

examples.de: Leon fragt den Experten nach einem Rat.
examples.en: Leon asks the expert for advice.

examples.de: Ich schenke meinem Neffen ein Buch.
examples.en: I give my nephew a book.

deeper.text: Many nationality words belong to this family, but not all of them. der Franzose (Frenchman) is an n-noun: Ich kenne einen Franzosen. der Italiener and der Spanier are normal nouns: Ich kenne einen Italiener. The ending of the word shows the difference: -e gets -n, -er does not.

example.de: Ich kenne einen Franzosen.
example.en: I know a Frenchman.

cards.more: Use the final -e as a hook and ask two quick questions. Is the noun masculine? Is it a person or an animal? If both answers are yes, you already hold half of the answer: just add -n. Try it with der Löwe: masculine, an animal, ends in -e, so den Löwen. Now try die Lampe: feminine, so nothing changes. The question about gender comes first, always.

cards.title: Three without -e: Mensch, Nachbar, Herr
cards.body: Three very common nouns do not end in -e but follow the pattern: der Mensch, der Nachbar, der Herr. After a consonant they add -en (Menschen), after r just -n (Nachbarn, Herrn). Only der Herr has a special plural: die Herren with -en.
cards.lead: Not every n-noun ends in -e. Three very common ones do not, and you meet them every day: Mensch, Nachbar and Herr. Look at what is added to each one.

examples.de: Frau Weber spricht mit dem Nachbarn.
examples.en: Frau Weber talks to the neighbour.

examples.de: Der Kellner fragt den Herrn: „Was möchten Sie trinken?“
examples.en: The waiter asks the gentleman: What would you like to drink?

examples.de: Viele Menschen essen bei Herrn Ali.
examples.en: Many people eat at Mr Ali's.

deeper.text: In everyday speech many people drop the -n with Nachbar and Mensch and say dem Nachbar or den Mensch. You will hear it, and nobody minds. In writing, in exams and in formal speech the -n is required, so train it from the start: dem Nachbarn, den Menschen.

example.de: Ich kenne meinen Nachbarn gut.
example.en: I know my neighbour well.

cards.more: Say the three pairs aloud as a rhythm: Mensch, Menschen. Nachbar, Nachbarn. Herr, Herrn. After the sounds sch the ending -en gets its own syllable, so it is easy to hear. After the sound r there is only a small -n. Only der Herr plays a trick: one Herr, two Herren, but dem Herrn in the singular. Say it with a number: ein Herr, zwei Herren, einem Herrn.

cards.title: Spot it in a sentence
cards.body: Look for the little word first: den, dem or des in front of a masculine noun is the signal. Then check the noun. If it is a group-one noun, it needs -n. The three sentences below show the three cases next to each other.
cards.lead: Now all three cases appear in real sentences. Find the signal word den, dem or des before each noun and check the -n at the end. The colours help you see the case.

examples.de: Mira trifft den Nachbarn.
examples.en: Mira meets the neighbour.

examples.de: Herr Ali gibt dem Kunden die Rechnung.
examples.en: Herr Ali gives the customer the bill.

examples.de: Das Handy des Kollegen ist kaputt.
examples.en: The colleague's mobile phone is broken.

deeper.text: The dative singular dem Kunden and the dative plural den Kunden look almost the same. Only the article shows the number: dem means one customer, den means several. So the article, not the noun, tells you singular or plural here. Listen for dem versus den in speech, because the -n is silent in the plural anyway.

example.de: Ich helfe den Kunden.
example.en: I help the customers.

cards.more: Be a detective with three clues. Clue one: find the article den, dem or des. Clue two: is the noun masculine and in the group of card three or four? Clue three: if yes, the noun must carry -n. If clue one is der or die, there is nothing to do. This also protects you from adding -n to the wrong words, such as der Lehrer. Only group-one nouns follow the rule.
steps: 1  Find the article: den, dem or des?
2  Is the noun masculine and one of the group nouns (Kollege, Kunde, Junge, Löwe, Neffe, Experte, Mensch, Nachbar, Herr)?
3  Then add -n or -en: den Nachbarn, dem Kunden, des Kollegen.

cards.title: Why „Herrn Ali“ and „Zum Löwen“
cards.body: A letter opens with Sehr geehrter Herr Ali, because the greeting is nominative. But Ich schreibe Herrn Ali eine E-Mail has the -n, because the dative needs it. The restaurant name „Zum Löwen“ hides the same rule: zum is zu dem, and der Löwe in the dative is dem Löwen.
cards.lead: Two things you saw for a long time now make sense. The -n in Herrn Ali and the -n in „Zum Löwen“ are the same rule you just learned. Here is the explanation.

examples.de: Sehr geehrter Herr Ali,
examples.en: Dear Mr Ali,

examples.de: Ich schreibe Herrn Ali eine E-Mail.
examples.en: I write Mr Ali an e-mail.

deeper.text: Not every noun ending in -e is an n-noun. der Käse is not a person, so it is a normal noun: der Preis des Käses, with -s in the genitive. The n-declension is mostly for living beings: people and animals. So the word Käse looks like Löwe, but it behaves differently.

example.de: Das ist der Preis des Käses.
example.en: That is the price of the cheese.

cards.more: Inns and restaurants in German-speaking countries often have a name with zum and an animal: Zum Löwen, Zum Bären. These names are old and always dative, because zum means zu dem and the place is at the lion. Now you can read the -n: it belongs to der Löwe and der Bär, which are both n-nouns. Next time you pass a restaurant called Zum Löwen, you will see today's rule on the sign.

lessons.title: Mira erklärt dem Praktikanten alles: n-declension (2)
lessons.goal: Decline n-nouns in -ent, -ant, -ist, -at, -oge, -graf (den Studenten, dem Praktikanten) and tell them from normal nouns such as der Chef.

grammar.point: Masculine nouns with a foreign ending for people (and a few others) follow the same pattern as group one: -ent (Student, Präsident), -ant (Praktikant, Elefant), -ist (Journalist, Polizist, Tourist), -at (Kandidat), -oge (Biologe, Psychologe), -graf (Fotograf). They take -en after a consonant and -n after -e in all cases except the nominative singular. Normal nouns such as der Lehrer, der Mann and der Chef do not. der Name and der Gedanke add -ns in the genitive (recognise only).

mistake.why: Nouns in -ent are n-nouns: they take -en in the accusative, dative and genitive. Only the nominative singular stays plain.

cards.title: Before we start: from 'den Kollegen' to 'den Praktikanten'
cards.body: Last lesson you learned group one: den Kollegen, dem Kunden. Today a second group joins: people with foreign endings, such as Student, Praktikant and Journalist. A new intern starts at Datenhafen, and Mira shows the intern everything. The rule is the same, only the nouns are new.
steps: You already know: der Student (the word) and Ich frage den Kollegen.
New today: Mira zeigt dem Praktikanten das Büro. Der Laptop des Studenten ist neu.
By the end you can: use -en after -ent, -ant, -ist, -at, -oge and -graf, and tell these nouns from normal ones such as der Chef.

examples.de: Ich frage den Kollegen.
examples.en: I ask the colleague.
examples.why: You know this: group one adds -n.

examples.de: Der Student ist nett.
examples.en: The student is nice.
examples.why: You know the word: the nominative has no ending.

examples.de: Mira zeigt dem Praktikanten das Büro.
examples.en: Mira shows the intern the office.
examples.why: New today: after a consonant the ending is -en.

examples.de: Der Laptop des Studenten ist neu.
examples.en: The student's laptop is new.
examples.why: New today: the genitive has -en, too.

cards.more: Think of two families. Group one is the family of the -e: Kollege, Kunde, Löwe, all with a small -n. Today's family is the family of the foreign endings: Student, Praktikant, Journalist, all with -en. They look different on the surface, but they play by the same rule: only the nominative stays plain, every other case wears the ending. You already know the rule, so you only learn the new family members.

cards.title: A new intern at Datenhafen
cards.body: A new Praktikant starts at Datenhafen today. A colleague asks Mira to look after the intern. Read the short scene and underline every Praktikant. When he is the one doing something, the noun is plain. In all other places it ends in -en.
cards.lead: A scene from the office at Datenhafen. Read it once and watch the word Praktikant. It appears with and without an ending. The next cards explain why.

examples.de: Kannst du dem Praktikanten das System zeigen?
examples.en: Can you show the intern the system?

examples.de: Ich erkläre dem Praktikanten alles.
examples.en: I explain everything to the intern.

examples.de: Der Praktikant fängt heute an.
examples.en: The intern starts today.

deeper.text: Do not mix up the two words: der Praktikant is the person, das Praktikum is the internship. Someone makes a Praktikum and is a Praktikant while he does it. Only the person word follows the n-declension: dem Praktikanten, but in dem Praktikum, a normal neuter noun.

example.de: Der Praktikant macht ein Praktikum bei Datenhafen.
example.en: The intern does an internship at Datenhafen.

cards.more: Play the scene as a film in your head. The colleague speaks to Mira, so the intern is only talked about: dem Praktikanten. Mira explains things, again to the intern: dem Praktikanten. But when the intern himself arrives, he is the one who acts: Der Praktikant fängt an. Each time he is on the receiving side the noun ends in -en. When he acts himself it stays plain.
steps: Kollegin: Mira, kannst du dem Praktikanten das System zeigen?
Mira: Klar, ich erkläre dem Praktikanten alles.
Kollegin: Danke. Der Praktikant fängt heute an.
Mira: Ich zeige dem Praktikanten zuerst das Büro.

cards.title: Foreign endings: -ent, -ant, -ist, -at, -oge, -graf
cards.body: Nouns for people with a foreign ending belong to group two: -ent, -ant, -ist, -at, -oge and -graf. The stress usually falls on the last syllable: Stu-DENT, Jour-na-LIST. Add -en after a consonant and -n after -e: der Biologe, den Biologen.
cards.lead: Group one was easy to spot, because it ends in -e. Group two has endings from Latin and Greek. Here is the list. Learn the endings, and you know the nouns.

examples.de: Der Polizist hilft dem Touristen.
examples.en: The police officer helps the tourist.

examples.de: Mira kennt den Studenten nicht.
examples.en: Mira does not know the student.

examples.de: Wir fragen den Fotografen.
examples.en: We ask the photographer.

deeper.text: The endings -ent, -ant and -ist come from Latin and Greek, and English has the same ones: student, assistant, tourist. That is a memory bridge. If an English word ends in -ent, -ant or -ist and the German twin is a person, it is almost always an n-noun. Even the elephant is one: der Elefant, den Elefanten.

example.de: Der Tourist sieht den Elefanten.
example.en: The tourist sees the elephant.

cards.more: Listen to the last syllable. In Student, Praktikant and Journalist the voice goes up on the last part: Stu-DENT, Prak-ti-KANT, Jour-na-LIST. That is the foreign-word melody. Whenever you hear it in a person word, your ear can tell you that the noun probably needs -en. Compare a native word such as Lehrer, which stresses the first part: LEH-rer. Stress is a good hint, not a law.

rows: der Student, der Präsident, der Assistent
der Journalist, der Polizist, der Tourist

cards.title: All cases of der Praktikant
cards.body: One noun, all cases: der Praktikant. In the accusative, dative and genitive it takes -en, and in the plural die Praktikanten. Nominative singular is the only plain form. It is the same pattern as der Kollege, only with -en after a consonant instead of -n.
cards.lead: Now you see the whole noun in one table, as you saw der Kollege in lesson four. Check where the plain form stands and where -en appears.

examples.de: Der Praktikant lernt schnell.
examples.en: The intern learns fast.

examples.de: Mira fragt den Praktikanten.
examples.en: Mira asks the intern.

examples.de: Das ist der Laptop des Praktikanten.
examples.en: That is the intern's laptop.

deeper.text: der Automat is an n-noun, too. A ticket machine in a station is der Automat, and you buy a ticket am Automaten, never am Automat. The word fits the family because it is a thing with a Latin ending and a person-like job. You will use it often at stations and shops.

example.de: Ich kaufe die Fahrkarte am Automaten.
example.en: I buy the ticket at the machine.

cards.more: Compare it with lesson four. There you added -n to a noun that already had an -e: Kollege became Kollegen. Here the noun has no -e, so the ending needs its own vowel: Praktikant becomes Praktikanten. The vowel makes the ending easier to say. Same rule, the letter e is simply provided by the ending instead of by the noun. Just as in Menschen, where you also said -en.

cards.title: Normal nouns that look similar
cards.body: Not every person word takes -n. der Lehrer, der Mann and der Chef stay the same in the accusative and dative: den Lehrer, dem Mann, den Chef. Ask two questions: does the noun end in -e? Does it have a foreign ending like -ent or -ist? If neither, it is a normal noun.
cards.lead: After two groups of n-nouns you may want to add -en everywhere. Stop: many masculine person words are normal. Here the contrast, so you know where not to add anything.

examples.de: Mira fragt den Chef.
examples.en: Mira asks the boss.

examples.de: Ich helfe dem Lehrer.
examples.en: I help the teacher.

examples.de: Wir kennen den Studenten und den Lehrer.
examples.en: We know the student and the teacher.

deeper.text: The genitive is a fast test. Normal masculine nouns add -s or -es in the genitive: des Lehrers, des Mannes, des Chefs. An n-noun never adds -s: des Studenten, des Kollegen. So if you can say des Mannes, it is a normal noun, and if you can say des Studenten, it is an n-noun.

example.de: Das ist der Laptop des Chefs.
example.en: That is the boss's laptop.

cards.more: Use a two-box sorting game. Box one: the n-nouns, with a very small number of members, all with -e or a foreign ending: Kollege, Kunde, Student, Journalist. Box two: everything else, and it is huge. Lehrer, Mann, Chef, Vater, Bruder, Sohn, Freund all belong there. If a masculine person word does not fit box one, drop it into box two and leave it alone. When unsure, ask which box.

cards.title: Two special nouns: der Name, der Gedanke
cards.body: Two nouns have a tiny difference in the genitive: der Name and der Gedanke. They add -n in the accusative and dative (den Namen, dem Namen), but -ns in the genitive: des Namens, des Gedankens. Recognise them when you read, you do not need to produce them yet.
cards.lead: A few nouns are n-nouns with one extra twist. The two you meet most often are der Name and der Gedanke. Look at the genitive column: it is the only different spot.

examples.de: Wie war Ihr Name?
examples.en: What was your name?

examples.de: Ich kenne den Namen nicht.
examples.en: I do not know the name.

examples.de: Der Klang des Namens ist schön.
examples.en: The sound of the name is beautiful.

deeper.text: A few more nouns behave like der Name. der Buchstabe (letter) becomes des Buchstabens and der Glaube (belief) becomes des Glaubens. You will see these in newspaper texts and in formal writing. In speech the genitive is rare, so you only need to read the -ns and understand it, not to say it.

example.de: Das ist der erste Buchstabe des Namens.
example.en: That is the first letter of the name.

cards.more: Think of the genitive as dressing up. An ordinary n-noun puts on one small ending, -n or -en. Name and Gedanke put on two small letters, -ns, as if the genitive -s and the n-ending came together: Namen plus s. It is only the genitive that does this. You will mostly read it in texts, like des Namens or des Gedankens. Do not worry about writing it now.

cards.title: Mixed practice in the office
cards.body: Now sort what you know. Group one: -e nouns and Mensch, Nachbar, Herr. Group two: -ent, -ant, -ist, -at, -oge, -graf. Normal nouns: all the others. In each sentence find the article, then decide which box the noun is in.
cards.lead: Everything together. In the office sentences below, colour and card order help you check the three boxes. Cover the table and decide for each noun: group one, group two or normal?

examples.de: Mira schreibt dem Journalisten eine E-Mail.
examples.en: Mira writes the journalist an e-mail.

examples.de: Der Chef sucht einen Kandidaten.
examples.en: The boss is looking for a candidate.

examples.de: Der Fotograf zeigt dem Kunden die Bilder.
examples.en: The photographer shows the customer the pictures.

deeper.text: The feminine twins are normal nouns: die Journalistin, die Fotografin, die Kandidatin. They never get -en in the singular and take -nen in the plural: die Journalistinnen. When a woman is meant, the problem disappears: Ich schreibe der Journalistin. For the men you need -en: Ich schreibe dem Journalisten.

example.de: Ich schreibe der Journalistin.
example.en: I write to the female journalist.

cards.more: Make it a three-question routine you run in your head for every masculine noun after den, dem or des. One: does it end in -e? Two: does it end in -ent, -ant, -ist, -at, -oge or -graf? Three: is it Mensch, Nachbar or Herr? If you answer yes even once, add the ending. If you answer no three times, the noun is normal and stays as it is.

lessons.title: Wie leben wir im Jahr 2050? A longer newspaper text
lessons.goal: Understand a longer newspaper text with simple strategies, use forecast phrases and talk about an article.

grammar.point: No new grammar: Futur and n-nouns in a real text. Reading strategy: headline and photo, the Vorspann as summary, W-questions, one key word per paragraph, do not stop at every unknown word. Forecast phrases: Experten erwarten, dass …, Laut einer Studie …, Man rechnet damit, dass …, voraussichtlich. In a dass-clause werden stands at the very end, after the infinitive. Trends: steigen, sinken, zunehmen, abnehmen, immer mehr.
grammar.oneLine: Laut Experten werden mehr Menschen im Homeoffice arbeiten.

mistake.wrong: Die Experten erwarten, dass mehr Menschen werden zu Hause arbeiten.
mistake.right: Die Experten erwarten, dass mehr Menschen zu Hause arbeiten werden.
mistake.why: In a dass-clause the finite verb stands last. With Futur that is werden, after the infinitive.

terms.meaning: the bold lead paragraph at the top of a newspaper article that gives the main facts
a statement about what will probably happen in the future

cards.title: Before we start: from short messages to a long article
cards.body: Until now your texts were short: messages, dialogues, a small advert. Real newspapers print longer texts with long sentences. Today Mira reads such a text in a Berlin newspaper, an article about life in the year 2050. There is no new grammar. You use what you know and learn how to read a long text.
steps: You already know: der Artikel, die Zeitung, die Studie.
New today: Laut Experten werden mehr Menschen im Homeoffice arbeiten.
By the end you can: read a longer newspaper text with a few simple strategies, use forecast phrases and talk about the article.

examples.de: Mira liest einen Artikel in der Zeitung.
examples.en: Mira reads an article in the newspaper.
examples.why: You know this: article and newspaper.

examples.de: Die Studie ist neu.
examples.en: The study is new.
examples.why: You know this word.

examples.de: Laut Experten werden mehr Menschen im Homeoffice arbeiten.
examples.en: According to experts, more people will work from home.
examples.why: New today: a forecast phrase from a newspaper.

cards.more: Think of a long newspaper article as a house with several rooms. Short texts were one-room flats: you saw everything at once. In a house you need a plan. Look at the front door first (the headline), then the hall (the lead paragraph), and then walk through the rooms one by one. You do not need to understand every piece of furniture to know what the house is for.

cards.title: Mira reads the article
cards.body: Mira reads an article from a Berlin newspaper. It has a headline, a bold lead paragraph called Vorspann and four short sections. The text does not give exact numbers: experts say what they expect. Read it once, without a dictionary, and watch the forecast phrases.
cards.lead: Here is the whole article in short form. Read it from top to bottom once. Look at the headline and the Vorspann first, then at the four sections. The next cards explain how to read it.

examples.de: Forscher erwarten, dass sich unser Alltag verändern wird.
examples.en: Researchers expect that our everyday life will change.

examples.de: Man rechnet damit, dass mehr ältere Menschen in der Stadt wohnen werden.
examples.en: It is expected that more older people will live in the city.

examples.de: In den Städten werden wohl mehr Menschen Fahrrad fahren.
examples.en: In the cities probably more people will ride bicycles.

deeper.text: German newspapers put the most important fact in the Vorspann, the bold lines in front of the text. If you read nothing else, read the Vorspann. It tells you who, what and when in two sentences, and the rest of the article only gives details. This is why you can understand a long text after reading only a few lines.

example.de: Im Vorspann steht die wichtigste Information.
example.en: The most important information is in the lead paragraph.

cards.more: Imagine you see the article in a shop window and have only ten seconds. You read the large headline, then the bold part, and that is already enough to tell a friend what the article is about. The four sections are like four drawers with details: you can open the one you like, for example Arbeit or Klima. You do not have to open all of them. A newspaper is built for fast readers.
steps: „Wie leben wir im Jahr 2050?“
Forscher erwarten, dass sich unser Alltag bis 2050 verändern wird. Wir haben mit Experten über Arbeit, Wohnen, Verkehr und Klima gesprochen.
Arbeit: Laut Experten werden mehr Menschen im Homeoffice arbeiten. Viele Büros werden kleiner sein.
Wohnen: Die Bevölkerung wird älter. Man rechnet damit, dass mehr ältere Menschen in der Stadt wohnen werden.
Verkehr: In den Städten werden wohl mehr Menschen Fahrrad fahren. Es ist zu erwarten, dass es mehr Elektroautos geben wird.
Klima: Voraussichtlich wird es im Sommer heißer. Viele Städte werden mehr Bäume haben.

cards.title: A reading strategy in five steps
cards.body: A long text is easier with a plan. First guess from the headline and the photo. Then read the Vorspann: it is the summary. Next ask the W-questions: wer, was, wann, wo. Mark one key word in each paragraph. Last rule: do not stop at every unknown word.
cards.lead: You have read the article once. Now use the same text to learn a way to read any long text. Follow the five steps below and test them on the headline and the first sentence.

examples.de: Wie leben wir im Jahr 2050?
examples.en: How will we live in the year 2050?

examples.de: Wir haben mit Experten über Arbeit, Wohnen, Verkehr und Klima gesprochen.
examples.en: We talked with experts about work, housing, traffic and climate.

examples.de: Viele Büros werden kleiner sein.
examples.en: Many offices will be smaller.

deeper.text: In an exam, read the questions before the text. Then you know what to look for, and you can scan the text for key words instead of understanding every line. You need only the parts that answer the questions. This saves time and nerves, and it is the way most people read a newspaper in everyday life as well.

example.de: Ich lese zuerst die Fragen.
example.en: I read the questions first.

cards.more: Compare it with looking for a flat in a new city. You do not read every street name. You look for the main road first, then for a few landmarks, and you ask a person when you are lost. In a text the main road is the Vorspann, the landmarks are your key words, and asking a person is the dictionary, which you use at the very end. Walk first, ask later.
steps: 1  Headline and photo: guess what the text is about.
2  Read the Vorspann: it is the short summary.
3  Ask wer, was, wann, wo, warum and look for the answers.
4  Find one key word in each paragraph.
5  Do not stop at every unknown word: guess from the sentence.

cards.title: Forecast language
cards.body: Newspapers do not say what will happen. They say what people expect. You will see Experten erwarten, dass …, Laut einer Studie …, Man rechnet damit, dass … and the word voraussichtlich. After dass the verb stands at the end, and werden comes after the infinitive.
cards.lead: The article is full of the same few phrases. They tell you that the writer is not sure. Look at the table, then find each phrase in the article from card two.

examples.de: Experten erwarten, dass es mehr Elektroautos geben wird.
examples.en: Experts expect that there will be more electric cars.

examples.de: Laut einer Studie werden mehr Menschen zu Hause arbeiten.
examples.en: According to a study, more people will work at home.

examples.de: Man rechnet damit, dass es im Sommer heißer wird.
examples.en: It is expected that it will get hotter in summer.

deeper.text: laut is a newspaper word. It takes the dative or the genitive: laut einer Studie, laut Experten. In speech people say die Experten sagen, dass … or Nach Ansicht der Experten sounds formal. If you hear laut in a conversation, it probably comes from the news. You will read it very often, but speak more simply.

example.de: Die Experten sagen, dass es heißer wird.
example.en: The experts say that it will get hotter.

cards.more: Sort the phrases by how sure the writer is. Experten erwarten, dass is fairly sure. Man rechnet damit is a little weaker. voraussichtlich means probably, and wohl also means probably. Es ist zu erwarten, dass … is the formal version of the first one, and you only need to recognise it. It is like a ladder from very sure to not so sure, and you climb up or down it depending on how much you trust the source.

rows: it is to be expected that …

cards.title: Long sentences unpacked
cards.body: Newspaper sentences can be long, but they are built from chunks. Cut the sentence at the commas. Find the main verb first: here werden in position two and arbeiten at the end. Then ask what each chunk says. The four chunks below form one single sentence.
cards.lead: A long sentence from the article, cut into four pieces. Read each piece alone, then put them together. You did the same with reading chunks in chapter five.

examples.de: Laut Experten werden in Zukunft mehr Menschen,
examples.en: According to experts, in future more people,

examples.de: die heute im Büro sitzen,
examples.en: who sit in the office today,

deeper.text: In a long sentence werden holds the first half and the infinitive the second half, like a bracket. Between them stands everything else. When you read, look for the second half of the bracket. As long as you have not found it, the sentence is not finished. This trick helps you in every long sentence with werden.

example.de: Mehr Menschen werden in zwanzig Jahren zu Hause arbeiten.
example.en: In twenty years more people will work from home.

cards.more: Imagine you must carry a long sentence upstairs. You cannot lift it all at once, so you carry it in chunks. First chunk: the main message. Second chunk: a small side comment between commas. Third chunk: the reason. Put them down in the right order and the sentence is easy. Always ask of a chunk: is this the main message, a comment or a reason? The commas show you where to cut.
steps: 1  Find the main verb: werden … arbeiten.
2  Cut at the commas: four chunks.
3  Ask of each chunk: message, comment or reason?
4  Put the chunks back together in your own words.

cards.title: Numbers and trends
cards.body: Articles talk about change. Use steigen (go up) and sinken (go down). The verbs zunehmen and abnehmen mean increase and decrease. Say immer mehr or immer weniger for more and more or less and less, and doppelt so viele for twice as many.
cards.lead: Forecasts are about change, and German has a small set of words for it. Here are the most common ones with examples. You will find the same words in graphs and in news.

examples.de: Die Lebenserwartung nimmt zu.
examples.en: Life expectancy is increasing.

examples.de: Der Verkehr in der Stadt nimmt ab.
examples.en: Traffic in the city is decreasing.

examples.de: Es gibt doppelt so viele Elektroautos wie vor fünf Jahren.
examples.en: There are twice as many electric cars as five years ago.

deeper.text: immer mehr means more and more and never takes an ending, even in front of a noun: immer mehr Menschen, not immer mehrere Menschen. You learned in chapter five that mehr and weniger never change. The same is true for immer mehr and immer weniger. They stay short in every case.

example.de: Immer mehr Menschen arbeiten zu Hause.
example.en: More and more people work at home.

cards.more: Take care with two small verbs. In texts about weather or traffic, zunehmen and abnehmen mean increase and decrease. But in everyday talk they are also used for weight: Ich habe zwei Kilo zugenommen means I gained two kilos, and Ich habe abgenommen means I lost weight. Do not be afraid when you hear them at the doctor. The idea is always more or less.

rows: more and more / less and less

cards.title: Talk about the article
cards.body: After reading you must be able to talk about the text. Use three chunks: Im Artikel geht es um … says what it is about. Der Autor meint, dass … gives his opinion. Überrascht hat mich, dass … says what surprised you. With dass the verb goes to the end.
cards.lead: Last card: you have read the article, and now you speak about it. Three chunks do most of the work. Learn them as blocks and add your own content.

examples.de: Im Artikel geht es um das Leben im Jahr 2050.
examples.en: The article is about life in the year 2050.

examples.de: Der Autor meint, dass mehr Menschen zu Hause arbeiten werden.
examples.en: The author thinks that more people will work at home.

examples.de: Überrascht hat mich, dass es mehr Elektroautos geben wird.
examples.en: What surprised me is that there will be more electric cars.

deeper.text: der Autor looks like a foreign word, but it is a normal noun: den Autor, dem Autor, des Autors. The plural moves the stress: die Autoren. The same is true for der Professor and der Doktor. Nouns in -or are not n-nouns, even if they look like Latin people words. So learn them with the genitive -s.

example.de: Ich kenne den Autor des Artikels.
example.en: I know the author of the article.

cards.more: Think of the three chunks as three pockets in your jacket. In the first pocket is the topic: Im Artikel geht es um. In the second pocket is somebody else's opinion: Der Autor meint, dass. In the third pocket is your own reaction: Überrascht hat mich, dass. When someone asks about a text, you pick one chunk from each pocket and you have three good sentences. Practise with any article you read this week.
