lessons.title: Die Freundin, der ich vertraue: relative clauses in the dative
lessons.goal: Use dem, der, dem and denen as relative pronouns: die Freundin, der ich vertraue; die Leute, denen ich danke.

grammar.point: The relative pronoun takes its case from its job inside the relative clause. If the verb needs a dative (helfen, danken, vertrauen, gehören, gefallen, begegnen, antworten, gratulieren) or the person receives something (geben, zeigen, erklären), the pronoun is dative: dem for masculine and neuter, der for feminine, denen for the plural. The verb stands at the end. English can drop the pronoun, German never does.
grammar.oneLine: Frau Weber ist die Nachbarin, der ich meine Pflanzen gebe.

mistake.wrong: Das sind die Freunde, den ich danke.
mistake.right: Das sind die Freunde, denen ich danke.
mistake.why: danken needs the dative, and the dative plural of the relative pronoun is the long form denen. den is only the article: den Freunden.

terms.meaning: the word after the comma that points back to a noun and starts the relative clause: der, die, das, dem, denen
a verb whose person object is in the dative: helfen, danken, vertrauen, gehören

cards.title: Before we start: from 'die Malerin, die ich mag' to 'die Nachbarin, der ich vertraue'
cards.body: In A2 you learned relative clauses for people who do something (der, die, das) and people you see or like (den, die, das). Today a third group joins: people you help, thank or trust. Anna leaves for Wien in March, and three people help her. You need one new word to describe them.
steps: You already know: Das ist die Malerin, die ich mag. A relative clause with die, verb at the end.
New today: Frau Weber ist die Nachbarin, der ich meine Pflanzen gebe. Das sind die Leute, denen ich danke.
By the end you can: use dem, der, dem and denen as relative pronouns and choose between der, den and dem.

examples.de: Das ist die Malerin, die ich mag.
examples.en: This is the painter I like.
examples.why: You know this: die is the accusative here, because I like her.

examples.de: Frau Weber ist die Nachbarin, der ich meine Pflanzen gebe.
examples.en: Frau Weber is the neighbour I give my plants to.
examples.why: New today: der is the dative of die, because I give the plants TO her.

examples.de: Das sind die Leute, denen ich danke.
examples.en: These are the people I thank.
examples.why: New today: denen is the dative plural, because danken takes the dative.

cards.more: Think of a relative clause as a small caption under a photo of a person. The caption says who this person is for you. Die Malerin, die ich mag is a caption about liking. Die Nachbarin, der ich vertraue is a caption about trust. Only one word changes, die becomes der, because the verb vertrauen needs the dative. Comma, pronoun, ich, verb at the end: all as before. You change one word and can name the people who matter to you.

cards.title: Who helps Anna with Wien?
cards.body: Anna leaves for Wien in March. Three people help her, and Anna describes each of them with a relative clause. Read the scene and look at the word after each comma: der, der, dem. Each one points back to a person and tells you what that person means to Anna.
cards.lead: A short scene in the WG kitchen with three people who help Anna. Read it once and look at the word after each comma. The next cards explain why it is der or dem and not die or den.

examples.de: Frau Weber ist die Nachbarin, der ich am meisten vertraue.
examples.en: Frau Weber is the neighbour I trust most.

examples.de: Mira ist die Freundin, der ich alle Fragen über Wien stelle.
examples.en: Mira is the friend I ask all my questions about Wien.

examples.de: Herr Ali ist der Mensch, dem ich sehr viel verdanke.
examples.en: Herr Ali is the person I owe a lot to.

deeper.text: English can leave the pronoun out: the friend I trust. German never can. You must always say who the clause points to: die Freundin, der ich vertraue. A German relative clause without der, dem or denen after the comma is simply not a sentence. The pronoun also carries the case, so it does more work than its English cousin.

example.de: Das ist die Freundin, der ich vertraue.
example.en: This is the friend I trust.

cards.more: Imagine three portrait frames on a wall, one for each helper. Under every frame hangs a small caption that says who this person is to Anna: the neighbour I trust, the friend I ask, the person I thank. Each caption is a relative clause, and each starts with a little word that points back at the portrait above it. You could write captions like this for the people in your life too. Today you learn that little word.
steps: Leon: Anna, wer gießt deine Zimmerpflanzen, wenn du in Wien bist?
Anna: Frau Weber. Sie ist die Nachbarin, der ich am meisten vertraue.
Leon: Und wer gibt dir Tipps für die Stadt?
Anna: Mira kommt aus Wien. Sie ist die Freundin, der ich alle Fragen über Wien stelle.
Leon: Und was macht Herr Ali?
Anna: Er macht eine Abschiedsfeier für mich. Er ist der Mensch, dem ich sehr viel verdanke.

cards.title: The dative row: dem, der, dem, denen
cards.body: Relative pronouns look like the definite article. You know the nominative and accusative rows from A2. The dative row is new: dem for masculine, der for feminine, dem for neuter and denen for the plural. Only the plural is different from the article, which is den.
cards.lead: You know der, die, das and den, die, das as relative pronouns. Now a third column is added, the dative. It is almost the article again, with one longer form in the plural.

examples.de: Das ist der Freund, dem ich vertraue.
examples.en: This is the friend I trust.

examples.de: Das ist die Freundin, der ich vertraue.
examples.en: This is the friend I trust.

examples.de: Das ist das Kind, dem Frau Weber hilft.
examples.en: This is the child Frau Weber helps.

deeper.text: Do not mix up two words. The article den goes with a noun and adds -n to it: den Freunden. The relative pronoun denen stands alone after the comma and opens the clause. In the next sentence you see both: the first is the article, the second the relative pronoun.

example.de: Ich helfe den Freunden, denen Mira schon geholfen hat.
example.en: I help the friends Mira has already helped.

cards.more: Count the letters. dem, der, dem have three letters each, exactly like the article. Only denen is longer, five letters, and only in the plural. Say it as a small rhythm: dem, der, dem, denen. Then say the nominative row you know: der, die, das, die. The dative row is the next verse of the same song, with one stretched note at the end. If you can sing the article, you can sing the relative pronoun.

cards.title: When is it dative?
cards.body: The case of the relative pronoun comes from its job inside the relative clause, not from the main clause. Ask what the verb of the relative clause needs. Dative verbs: helfen, danken, vertrauen, gehören, gefallen, begegnen, antworten, gratulieren. Also a person who receives something: jemandem etwas geben, zeigen, erklären.
cards.lead: The last card showed the forms. This card shows how to choose between them. You do not look at the main clause, you look at the verb inside the relative clause.

examples.de: Frau Weber ist die Nachbarin, der ich meine Pflanzen gebe.
examples.en: Frau Weber is the neighbour I give my plants to.

examples.de: Mira ist die Freundin, der ich alles erklären kann.
examples.en: Mira is the friend I can explain everything to.

examples.de: Das sind die Leute, denen ich danke.
examples.en: These are the people I thank.

deeper.text: Gefallen turns the English sentence around. The thing is the subject, the person who likes it is dative: Die Stadt gefällt mir. In a relative clause you get two possibilities. If the person is the one you point to, use the dative: der Freund, dem die Stadt gefällt. If the thing is the one you point to, use the nominative: die Stadt, die mir gefällt.

example.de: Das ist der Freund, dem die Stadt gefällt.
example.en: This is the friend who likes the city.

cards.more: Try a question test. Cover the relative pronoun and ask a question about the person with the verb of the relative clause. Ich vertraue ... : wem vertraue ich? The question word wem tells you: dative, so dem, der or denen. Ich kenne ... : wen kenne ich? The question word wen tells you: accusative, so den, die or das. It takes two seconds and works with every verb, even new ones that you have never seen before.
steps: 1  Take the second sentence without the pronoun: Ich vertraue der Nachbarin.
2  Ask: wem vertraue ich? Wem means dative.
3  Gender and number come from the noun you point to: die Nachbarin is feminine, so der.
4  Move the pronoun to the front and the verb to the end: …, der ich vertraue.

cards.title: Nominative, accusative or dative?
cards.body: One noun, three jobs. The main clause does not decide, the relative clause does. Does the person act (nominative), is the person seen, known or asked (accusative), or does the person receive, get help or thanks (dative)? Remember der Nachbar: in the main clause it takes -n: den Nachbarn, dem Nachbarn.
cards.lead: Now you put all three columns side by side with the same noun. The table shows how the job in the relative clause changes the pronoun while the main clause stays the same.

examples.de: Ich kenne den Nachbarn, der im dritten Stock wohnt.
examples.en: I know the neighbour who lives on the third floor.

examples.de: Ich besuche den Nachbarn, den Anna gut kennt.
examples.en: I visit the neighbour whom Anna knows well.

examples.de: Ich danke dem Nachbarn, dem Anna vertraut.
examples.en: I thank the neighbour whom Anna trusts.

deeper.text: In a relative clause with a verb that takes two objects, the person is dative and the thing is accusative. You have one pronoun for the person, and the thing stays a normal noun with its article: die Kollegin, der ich das Buch gebe. Do not use die here, even though the colleague is feminine and you may think of her as the one you give.

example.de: Das ist die Kollegin, der Mira das Buch gibt.
example.en: This is the colleague Mira gives the book to.

cards.more: Think of a stage play. The relative pronoun is an actor with a role in the little play inside the comma. The role decides the costume: a main role, der, a role that is seen, den, or a role that receives, dem. The big play around it, the main clause, has its own actors and costumes. Same noun, same actor, but he changes his costume for each little play. Ask: what is his role inside the commas?

rows: Das ist der Nachbar, der Anna hilft.
Das ist der Nachbar, den ich gut kenne.
He receives, is helped, is thanked (Dativ)
Das ist der Nachbar, dem ich vertraue.

cards.title: Denen: the plural trap
cards.body: In the plural the dative relative pronoun is denen, never den. This is the one place where the pronoun is longer than the article. Look at the verb: schreiben, erklären, helfen all need a person in the dative, so a plural noun gets denen: die Freunde, denen ich schreibe.
cards.lead: You have seen denen twice. This card shows why it is the most common mistake: the article den looks so similar. We put them side by side and train your eye.

examples.de: Das sind die Freunde, denen ich oft schreibe.
examples.en: These are the friends I often write to.

examples.de: Das sind die Kollegen, denen Mira alles erklärt.
examples.en: These are the colleagues Mira explains everything to.

examples.de: Das sind die Nachbarn, denen Frau Weber hilft.
examples.en: These are the neighbours Frau Weber helps.

deeper.text: A relative clause can also sit inside the main clause. Then it has a comma on both sides, and the main verb follows right after the second comma. The pronoun still points to the noun in front of it. This makes your sentences richer, but only if you keep the commas: a comma before and after the clause.

example.de: Die Freunde, denen ich schreibe, wohnen in Madrid.
example.en: The friends I write to live in Madrid.

cards.more: Hold two cards in your hands. On the left card the article den, short, followed by a noun with -n: den Freunden. On the right card the relative pronoun denen, longer, followed by a comma and a clause. When you write a plural relative clause, ask yourself: which card do I hold? If the next word is a noun, you need the left card. If the next word is the subject of a clause, you need the right card.

cards.title: Describing people precisely
cards.body: With the dative row you can describe the people around you in one sentence: who helps you, who you thank, whom you trust. Pick the verb that fits and let it choose the pronoun. These verbs are the most useful: helfen, danken, vertrauen, gehören, gefallen, begegnen, antworten, gratulieren.
cards.lead: You have all the pieces: the forms, the choice and the plural. Now you practise on real descriptions. Each sentence says in one go who a person is and what they mean to you.

examples.de: Herr Ali ist der Chef, dem Leon in der Küche hilft.
examples.en: Herr Ali is the boss Leon helps in the kitchen.

examples.de: Mira ist die Freundin, der Anna alles erzählt.
examples.en: Mira is the friend Anna tells everything.

examples.de: Das sind die Menschen, denen Anna am meisten dankt.
examples.en: These are the people Anna thanks most.

deeper.text: Verdanken is for good things only: you owe someone your success, your job or your luck. Ich verdanke Herrn Ali viel means that Herr Ali made something possible for me. Note that Herr takes -n in the dative, as in all cases except the nominative: Herrn Ali. You can use it with a relative clause for a mentor, a teacher or a helper.

example.de: Er ist der Mensch, dem ich viel verdanke.
example.en: He is the person I owe a lot to.

cards.more: Build a little portrait of one person in three steps. First the noun: die Freundin. Then the verb that fits the person: vertrauen, danken, helfen. Then the pronoun that the verb chooses: der. Say it aloud as a chain: die Freundin, der ich vertraue. Do the same for two people from your life. When you can build the chain without the table, you own the dative relative clause. Use the table only to check.

lessons.title: Die Wohnung, in der ich wohnen werde: preposition + relative pronoun
lessons.goal: Describe things and places precisely with in der, mit dem, für die, auf den and von denen, and use wo for places.

grammar.point: A preposition stands in front of the relative pronoun, as one block: die Wohnung, in der ich wohne. The preposition decides the case (mit, bei, von, zu, aus: dative; für, durch, gegen, ohne, um: accusative; in, an, auf: dative for wo?, accusative for wohin?), the noun decides gender and number. The verb stands at the end. Verbs with a fixed preposition work the same way. In spoken German, wo can replace preposition plus pronoun for places.
grammar.oneLine: Das ist die Wohnung, in der Anna wohnen wird.

mistake.wrong: Das ist die Wohnung, der ich in wohne.
mistake.right: Das ist die Wohnung, in der ich wohne.
mistake.why: The preposition comes first, then the relative pronoun. German never leaves the preposition at the end, as English can: the flat I live in.

terms.meaning: a small word such as in, mit, für or auf that stands in front of a noun or pronoun and decides its case
a preposition such as in, an or auf that takes the dative for wo? and the accusative for wohin?

cards.title: Before we start: from 'die Freundin, der ich vertraue' to 'die Stadt, in der ich wohne'
cards.body: In lesson 7 the pronoun came straight after the comma. Today a small word moves in front of it: a preposition. Anna looks for a flat in Wien and wants to describe it exactly: the flat in which she will live, the studio for which she wants to work. It is one step more, and you already know every part.
steps: You already know: Ich wohne in der Stadt. and Die Freundin, der ich vertraue (lesson 7).
New today: Das ist die Wohnung, in der Anna wohnen wird. Das Atelier, für das sie arbeiten möchte, liegt in Wien.
By the end you can: put the preposition in front of the relative pronoun, take the case from the preposition, and use wo for places.

examples.de: Ich wohne in der Stadt.
examples.en: I live in the city.
examples.why: You know this: in plus the dative, as in a normal sentence.

examples.de: Das ist die Wohnung, in der Anna wohnen wird.
examples.en: This is the flat Anna will live in.
examples.why: New today: in der points back to die Wohnung.

examples.de: Das ist das Atelier, für das Anna arbeiten möchte.
examples.en: This is the studio Anna would like to work for.
examples.why: New today: für das, because für takes the accusative.

cards.more: Think of the preposition as a bodyguard for the pronoun. In lesson 7 the pronoun walked to the front alone: der ich vertraue. Now the bodyguard comes along: in der ich wohne, mit dem ich arbeite. Two words, one block, and they never separate. English lets the bodyguard stay behind: the flat I live in. German keeps the pair together at the front of the clause, and the verb still goes last.

cards.title: A flat in Wien
cards.body: Anna looks at flat ads in Wien, and Mira, who knows the city, helps her. Read the scene and underline every pair of preposition and pronoun: in der, in dem, mit der, für das. Each pair opens a relative clause, and the verb waits at the end.
cards.lead: A scene with Anna and Mira at the laptop. Read it once and look at the two words after each comma. The next cards explain how they are built and why they look the way they do.

examples.de: Das ist die Wohnung, in der ich wohnen möchte.
examples.en: This is the flat I would like to live in.

examples.de: Das ist das Viertel, in dem ich aufgewachsen bin.
examples.en: This is the neighbourhood I grew up in.

examples.de: Die Vermieterin, mit der ich telefoniert habe, war sehr nett.
examples.en: The landlady I spoke to on the phone was very nice.

deeper.text: In normal sentences German likes short forms: im Viertel, am Fluss, zum Bahnhof. In a relative clause the pronoun is a full word, so a short form is not possible: das Viertel, in dem ich wohne, never im ich wohne. Always write the long form, in dem, an dem, zu dem. Then you cannot go wrong.

example.de: Das ist das Viertel, in dem ich wohne.
example.en: This is the neighbourhood I live in.

cards.more: Picture a flat ad as a short list of captions. Every line describes one thing: the flat, the room, the landlady, the neighbourhood. Each caption starts with the noun and then adds a clause that says more: the flat in which, the room in which, the landlady with whom. The little pair after the comma is the hook. It catches the noun and holds the rest of the sentence. Read the scene aloud and listen to the hooks.
steps: Anna: Schau mal, Mira. Das ist die Wohnung, in der ich wohnen möchte. Sie hat ein Zimmer, in dem ich malen kann.
Mira: Schön! Und das Viertel? Das ist das Viertel, in dem ich aufgewachsen bin. In Wien sagen wir Grätzl.
Anna: Grätzl! Das gefällt mir. Die Vermieterin, mit der ich telefoniert habe, war sehr nett.
Mira: Dann ruf sie bald an. Das Atelier, für das du arbeiten wirst, hilft dir sicher bei der Suche.

cards.title: Preposition first
cards.body: A relative clause with a preposition is built from two sentences. Take the preposition out of the second sentence and put it right after the comma, in front of the pronoun. The preposition decides the case, the noun decides gender and number, and the verb goes last.
cards.lead: You have seen the finished clauses. Now you see how to build one from two simple sentences, step by step. You can use this recipe for any preposition and any noun.

examples.de: Das ist die Wohnung, in der Anna wohnen wird.
examples.en: This is the flat Anna will live in.

examples.de: Ich kenne den Mann, mit dem Mira spricht.
examples.en: I know the man Mira is talking to.

examples.de: Das ist der Park, in dem wir oft spazieren gehen.
examples.en: This is the park we often walk in.

deeper.text: English can put the preposition at the end of the sentence: the flat I live in. German never can. The preposition always stands in front of the relative pronoun, as one block, and nothing else may come between them. A sentence like die Wohnung, der ich in wohne is wrong in German, however natural the English order feels.

example.de: Das ist die Wohnung, in der ich wohne.
example.en: This is the flat I live in.

cards.more: Think of a lift with two doors. The preposition is the person who enters first, the pronoun follows. They stand in the lift together, and the doors close: nobody can squeeze in between them, and nobody can stay behind. The lift goes to the front of the clause. Only then does the subject step in, and the verb goes to the last floor. The order of the passengers never changes: preposition, pronoun, subject, verb.
steps: 1  Two sentences: Das ist die Wohnung. Anna wird in der Wohnung wohnen.
2  Find the preposition in the second sentence: in. Put it right after the comma.
3  The preposition decides the case: in plus wo? takes the dative.
4  Gender and number come from the noun you point to: die Wohnung is feminine, so der.
5  The verb goes to the end: Das ist die Wohnung, in der Anna wohnen wird.

cards.title: Dative prepositions
cards.body: Some prepositions always take the dative: mit, bei, von, zu, aus, nach, seit. After them the pronoun is dem, der or denen: mit dem, bei der, zu denen. The two-way prepositions in, an and auf also take the dative when the question is wo?: in der, in dem.
cards.lead: The recipe says the preposition decides the case. Here are the dative prepositions you already know, now with their relative pronouns, and the two-way prepositions for places where something is.

examples.de: Das ist die Vermieterin, mit der Anna telefoniert hat.
examples.en: This is the landlady Anna spoke to on the phone.

examples.de: Das ist das Land, aus dem Ben kommt.
examples.en: This is the country Ben comes from.

examples.de: Das ist die Firma, bei der Mira arbeitet.
examples.en: This is the company Mira works for.

deeper.text: Two-way prepositions ask for two cases. With wo? (a place where something is) they take the dative: die Stadt, in der Anna wohnt. With wohin? (a goal, a movement) they take the accusative: die Stadt, in die Anna zieht. The relative clause follows the same test as an ordinary sentence. Ask the question first, then pick the pronoun.

example.de: Wien ist die Stadt, in die Anna im März zieht.
example.en: Wien is the city Anna is moving to in March.

cards.more: Learn the dative prepositions as a short chant: aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu. Whenever one of them stands in front of a relative pronoun, the case is dative, and you never have to think about the verb. For in, an and auf, ask yourself a question: wo? or wohin? Where is something, the dative, in der. Where does something go, the accusative, in die. Two questions, two answers, always the same.

cards.title: Accusative prepositions and verbs with prepositions
cards.body: After für, durch, gegen, ohne and um the accusative is fixed: für den, für die, für das. Verbs with a fixed preposition work the same way: the preposition goes in front of the pronoun and decides the case. warten auf, denken an and sprechen über all take the accusative.
cards.lead: The dative group is done. Now the accusative group, and the verbs you learned with a fixed preposition in B1 chapter four. They also move in front of the pronoun and choose the case.

examples.de: Das ist der Bus, auf den ich warte.
examples.en: This is the bus I am waiting for.

examples.de: Mira ist die Freundin, an die Anna oft denkt.
examples.en: Mira is the friend Anna often thinks of.

examples.de: Das Atelier, für das Anna arbeiten möchte, liegt in Wien.
examples.en: The studio Anna would like to work for is in Wien.

deeper.text: The preposition belongs to the verb, not to the pronoun, so you must know it. sich freuen auf is for something that is coming, sich freuen über for something that is here. The relative clause does not change this: die Reise, auf die ich mich freue, but das Geschenk, über das ich mich freue. If you change the verb, the preposition and the case may change with it.

example.de: Das ist die Reise, auf die sich Anna freut.
example.en: This is the trip Anna is looking forward to.

cards.more: Treat the verb with its preposition as one unit that you already know: warten auf, denken an, sprechen über. When you build a relative clause, simply take the preposition out of the unit and put it in front of the pronoun. The verb stays at the end. Warten auf den Bus becomes der Bus, auf den ich warte. Nothing is lost on the way. The case came with the preposition from the beginning, and you only moved it.

rows: der Bus, auf den ich warte
die Freundin, an die ich denke
das Thema, über das wir sprechen
die Reise, auf die ich mich freue
das Atelier, für das Anna arbeiten möchte
der Beruf, von dem er träumt

cards.title: Wo for places
cards.body: In spoken German wo often replaces preposition plus pronoun when the noun is a place: die Stadt, wo ich wohne means die Stadt, in der ich wohne. Use wo only for places, such as a city, a flat or a restaurant. Never use it for people or things: not die Freundin, wo ich vertraue.
cards.lead: Now a shortcut that you hear all the time in spoken German. It saves you the preposition and the gender, but it works only in one situation: when the noun is a place.

examples.de: Das ist die Stadt, wo Anna wohnen wird.
examples.en: This is the city where Anna will live.

examples.de: Das ist das Restaurant, wo Leon samstags kocht.
examples.en: This is the restaurant where Leon cooks on Saturdays.

examples.de: Das ist das Viertel, wo ich aufgewachsen bin.
examples.en: This is the neighbourhood where I grew up.

deeper.text: After alles, etwas and nichts a relative clause starts with was, not das: Das ist alles, was ich brauche. You will often read this in texts and hear it in conversation. You do not need to use it yet, it is enough to recognise it. The same is true after a whole sentence: was means which, in a general sense.

example.de: Das ist alles, was ich brauche.
example.en: That is all I need.

cards.more: Think of two doors to the same room. The written door says in der. The spoken door says wo. Both lead into the city, the flat or the café, so you can use either. But the spoken door only opens for rooms, for places. If the noun is a person, the door stays shut. A quick test: can you ask Wo? about the noun? Wo wohnt Anna? Yes. Wo vertraut Anna? No, so no wo. Use in der whenever you are not sure.

das Viertel, in dem ich aufgewachsen bin
das Viertel, wo ich aufgewachsen bin
das Restaurant, in dem Leon kocht

cards.title: Describe your dream flat
cards.body: Now describe your own dream flat. Use two or three relative clauses, one with in, one with für, mit or auf. Start with Ich suche or Ich möchte, name the thing, and add a clause for what you want to do or have there. Preposition first, verb last.
cards.lead: You know the recipe, the case rules and the shortcut. Here you put them together in a short wish list, the way you would in a flat ad or in a conversation with a landlady.

examples.de: Ich suche eine Wohnung, in der ich malen kann.
examples.en: I am looking for a flat in which I can paint.

examples.de: Ich möchte ein Viertel, in dem es viele Cafés gibt.
examples.en: I would like a neighbourhood in which there are many cafés.

examples.de: Ich wünsche mir eine Vermieterin, auf die ich mich verlassen kann.
examples.en: I wish for a landlady I can rely on.

deeper.text: You may also read dessen and deren in texts. They mean whose: die Malerin, deren Bilder in Wien hängen. These are genitive forms of the relative pronoun. You do not need to produce them, only to recognise them when you read. Then you will understand a sentence that otherwise looks as if a word were missing.

example.de: Anna ist die Malerin, deren Bilder in Wien hängen.
example.en: Anna is the painter whose pictures hang in Wien.

cards.more: Make a shopping list for a flat. Write one line for each thing you want: a kitchen in which we can cook together, a neighbourhood in which there is a park, a landlady on whom I can rely. Each line has the same shape: noun, comma, preposition, pronoun, subject, verb at the end. Writing five lines is the best practice you can do now. Once the shape feels natural, you can add the words you like most.
steps: 1  Name what you want: Ich suche eine Wohnung
2  Add a comma, the preposition and the pronoun: , in der
3  Say what you want to do or have there, verb last: ich malen kann.

lessons.title: Meine Vision: eine Welt, in der …
lessons.goal: Talk and write about visions of the future with Futur, Konjunktiv II and relative clauses: Ich stelle mir eine Welt vor, in der …

grammar.topic: Talking about visions (use of Futur, Konjunktiv II and relative clauses)
grammar.point: No new grammar. A vision uses Ich stelle mir … vor with mir (dative sich), a relative clause with or without a preposition (eine Welt, in der …), Futur for what you expect (In 20 Jahren werden …), Konjunktiv II for dreams (Es wäre schön, wenn …) and dass-clauses with werden at the end (Ich hoffe, dass …). Comparatives and superlatives in front of nouns need their endings.
grammar.oneLine: Ich stelle mir eine Welt vor, in der alle glücklich sind.

mistake.wrong: Ich stelle mich eine Welt vor, in der alle glücklich sind.
mistake.right: Ich stelle mir eine Welt vor, in der alle glücklich sind.
mistake.why: To imagine something is sich (Dat) etwas vorstellen: the sich is dative, mir. Ich stelle mich vor means I introduce myself.

terms.meaning: a picture of the future that you imagine or wish for
the verb form for wishes and dreams: würde, wäre, hätte

cards.title: Before we start: from 'Ich träume von …' to 'Ich stelle mir eine Welt vor, in der …'
cards.body: You can already say what you dream of: Ich träume von einem Haus am Meer. Today you go one step bigger. You describe a whole world, a city or a life, with a relative clause: a world in which, a city in which. No new grammar, only the pieces from this chapter put together to talk about the future.
steps: You already know: Ich träume von einem Haus am Meer. and Das ist die Wohnung, in der Anna wohnen wird.
New today: Ich stelle mir eine Stadt vor, in der niemand ein Auto braucht. In 20 Jahren werden wir weniger Müll haben.
By the end you can: describe a vision of the future, say whether it is a hope or a dream, and write a short vision text.

examples.de: Ich träume von einem Haus am Meer.
examples.en: I dream of a house by the sea.
examples.why: You know this: träumen von plus the dative.

examples.de: Das ist die Wohnung, in der Anna wohnen wird.
examples.en: This is the flat Anna will live in.
examples.why: You know this: preposition plus pronoun (lesson 8).

examples.de: Ich stelle mir eine Stadt vor, in der niemand ein Auto braucht.
examples.en: I imagine a city in which nobody needs a car.
examples.why: New today: the two pieces together, as a vision.

cards.more: Think of a vision as a postcard from the future. You are standing in the year 2046, and you write home about what you see: the city in which nobody drives, the people with whom you live, the work that you do. Every sentence on the postcard is a relative clause or a werden-sentence that you already know. The only new thing is the idea that you are the one who writes the postcard.

cards.title: Visions at the WG table
cards.body: At the WG table everybody tells their vision for the future. Four people, four short statements. Read them and underline the relative clauses and every werden. Notice that a vision is made from what you already know: relative clauses, Futur and a few fixed phrases.
cards.lead: A scene at the WG table. Four people say what their world looks like in 20 years. Read it once and look for the pieces you know. The next cards sort the patterns and explain them.

examples.de: Ich stelle mir eine Welt vor, in der Technik allen Menschen hilft.
examples.en: I imagine a world in which technology helps all people.

examples.de: Mein Traum ist ein Restaurant, in dem alle Gäste an einem Tisch sitzen.
examples.en: My dream is a restaurant in which all guests sit at one table.

examples.de: Ich hoffe, dass wir in 20 Jahren weniger Müll haben werden.
examples.en: I hope that we will have less waste in 20 years.

deeper.text: In 20 Jahren means 20 years from now: in plus the dative. 20 years ago is vor 20 Jahren. Both use the same noun in the dative plural, only the preposition changes. This is how you place a vision in time. You will often need both in one text: Vor 20 Jahren gab es noch keine Smartphones wie heute. In 20 Jahren ...

example.de: Vor 20 Jahren gab es noch keine Smartphones wie heute.
example.en: 20 years ago there were no smartphones like today.

cards.more: Imagine the four statements as four windows of a house, each with a different view. Mira looks out at technology, Ben at less waste, Leon at a shared table, Anna at a lively neighbourhood. All four windows are built from the same frame: a wish, a comma and a clause with a pronoun or dass. If you can describe one window, you can describe all of them. Your own view out of the window is the next step.
steps: Mira: Ich stelle mir eine Welt vor, in der Technik allen Menschen hilft.
Ben: Ich hoffe, dass wir in 20 Jahren weniger Müll haben werden.
Leon: Mein Traum ist ein Restaurant, in dem alle Gäste an einem Tisch sitzen.
Anna: Ich stelle mir ein Viertel vor, in dem Maler, Kinder und alte Menschen zusammen wohnen.

cards.title: Vision patterns
cards.body: Four patterns are enough for most visions. Ich stelle mir … vor with mir, never mich, followed by a relative clause. In 20 Jahren wird … for what you expect. Ich hoffe, dass … with werden at the end. Mein Traum ist …, in dem … for a dream with a place.
cards.lead: The scene showed the patterns in action. Here they are in one table, so you can pick the one that fits your idea. Each one is built from a piece you have already learned.

examples.de: Ich stelle mir eine Stadt vor, in der niemand ein Auto braucht.
examples.en: I imagine a city in which nobody needs a car.

examples.de: In 20 Jahren werden die meisten Menschen weniger arbeiten.
examples.en: In 20 years most people will work less.

examples.de: Mein Traum ist eine Welt, in der alle genug zu essen haben.
examples.en: My dream is a world in which everybody has enough to eat.

deeper.text: Two verbs look alike but use sich in different cases. Ich stelle mir etwas vor means I imagine something: mir is dative, the thing is the object. Ich stelle mich vor means I introduce myself: mich is accusative. One letter changes the meaning completely. So Ich stelle mir vor, dass … always uses mir, never mich.

example.de: Ich stelle mich vor: Ich bin Anna.
example.en: I introduce myself: I am Anna.

cards.more: Think of the four patterns as four small boxes with labels. The first box is for pictures, the second for predictions, the third for hopes, the fourth for dreams with a place. When you want to say something about the future, first ask which box it belongs to. Do you see a picture in your head? Take the first. Do you expect it? The second. Do you hope for it? The third. Then fill the box.

rows: Ich stelle mir … vor, in der/dem …
Ich stelle mir eine Stadt vor, in der niemand ein Auto braucht.
In 20 Jahren werden die meisten Menschen weniger arbeiten.
Ich hoffe, dass es mehr Frieden geben wird.
Mein Traum ist eine Welt, in der alle genug zu essen haben.

cards.title: Realistic or a dream?
cards.body: Futur and Konjunktiv II say different things. Ich werde … means I expect it, I think it will happen. Ich würde … or Es wäre schön, wenn … means I wish it, it is a dream. Choose the form that matches how sure you are, and the listener will understand your attitude.
cards.lead: In your visions you may be certain or you may only wish. German shows the difference with the verb form. This card puts the two side by side, so you can feel the difference in meaning.

examples.de: In 20 Jahren werde ich wohl in Berlin wohnen.
examples.en: In 20 years I will probably live in Berlin.

examples.de: Es wäre schön, wenn alle Menschen mehr Zeit hätten.
examples.en: It would be nice if all people had more time.

examples.de: Ich würde gern in einer Stadt ohne Autos leben.
examples.en: I would like to live in a city without cars.

deeper.text: German speakers often soften a vision with wahrscheinlich or vielleicht and still use Futur. Ich werde wahrscheinlich in Wien bleiben says what you expect, but you are not sure. Vielleicht werden wir uns oft sehen is a hope with a little doubt. This is more natural than saying Ich werde in Wien bleiben, as if it were certain.

example.de: Wahrscheinlich werden wir in 20 Jahren weniger Auto fahren.
example.en: We will probably drive less in 20 years.

cards.more: Picture a traffic light for the future. Green is Futur: Ich werde … I am sure enough to go. Yellow is Futur with wahrscheinlich or wohl: I think so, but not completely. Red is not a stop sign here, it is the dream: Ich würde … or Es wäre schön, wenn … I would like it, but I do not promise. The more you wish and the less you expect, the closer you move to the dream form.

rows: I expect it, I think it will happen
In 20 Jahren werde ich in Wien wohnen.
I think so, but I am not sure
Ich werde wahrscheinlich in Wien bleiben.
I wish it, it is a dream
Es wäre schön, wenn alle mehr Zeit hätten.

cards.title: Bigger, greener, fairer
cards.body: Visions love comparatives and superlatives in front of nouns: eine gerechtere Welt, sauberere Städte, die wichtigste Veränderung. You know the endings from chapter five: comparative -er plus the ending, superlative -st plus the ending. Check the article, then put the ending behind the comparative or superlative.
cards.lead: A vision usually says that things will be better, greener or fairer. For this you need the comparatives before a noun that you practised in chapter five. Here they come back in the world of ideas.

examples.de: Ich wünsche mir eine gerechtere Welt.
examples.en: I wish for a fairer world.

examples.de: In 20 Jahren wird es sauberere Städte geben.
examples.en: In 20 years there will be cleaner cities.

examples.de: Das ist die wichtigste Veränderung für unsere Zukunft.
examples.en: That is the most important change for our future.

deeper.text: From gerecht you can form die Gerechtigkeit, justice. The ending is -igkeit, an extended form of -keit, like die Müdigkeit from müde. After adjectives in -ig, -lich or -bar the plain -keit is enough: die Möglichkeit from möglich. It is the same word-family pattern you saw in chapter five. Nouns in -keit are always feminine, so it is die Gerechtigkeit.

example.de: Gerechtigkeit ist für Anna das wichtigste Ziel.
example.en: Justice is the most important goal for Anna.

cards.more: Say the sentences twice. First with an adjective alone: Die Welt ist gerecht. Then with a noun after it: eine gerechtere Welt. The first sentence is a statement, the second is a picture. In the picture, the adjective needs its ending, and the comparative takes one more -er in front of it. Wish lists are full of these: bessere, grünere, ruhigere, gerechtere. Make three of your own and check each ending against the article.

cards.title: Writing a vision text
cards.body: A vision text has three parts. An opening that says when and where. Three short pictures, for example work, living and people. A closing with a hope. Write in simple present and use werden only once or twice to place the vision in time. Use relative clauses for the details.
cards.lead: You know how to say a vision in one sentence. Now you write a whole text. The recipe below tells you what to put where, so you do not have to start from a blank page.

examples.de: In 20 Jahren werde ich in einer ruhigen Stadt leben.
examples.en: In 20 years I will live in a quiet city.

examples.de: Die Menschen, mit denen ich zusammenlebe, sind meine Freunde.
examples.en: The people I live with are my friends.

examples.de: Ich hoffe, dass dieser Traum wahr wird.
examples.en: I hope that this dream comes true.

deeper.text: A vision text sounds heavy if every sentence has werden. Native speakers use Futur once at the start, to set the time, and then describe the picture in the present, as in a report from the future: In 20 Jahren wird die Stadt grün sein. Es gibt viele Parks, und niemand braucht ein Auto. The first sentence sets the scene, and the present tense makes it vivid.

example.de: In 20 Jahren wird die Stadt grün sein, und niemand braucht ein Auto.
example.en: In 20 years the city will be green, and nobody needs a car.

cards.more: Think of a vision text as a short film in three scenes. Scene one is the establishing shot: when and where are we? Scenes two, three and four are three close-ups: one at work, one at home, one with the people. The final shot is the hope, and the music swells. If you write one sentence for each scene, you already have six to eight sentences. Add one relative clause to every scene and the text feels like a story.
steps: 1  Opening: When and where? In 20 Jahren werde ich in … leben.
2  Picture one, work: Ich arbeite in einer Firma, in der …
3  Picture two, living: Ich wohne in einer Wohnung, in der …
4  Picture three, people: Die Menschen, mit denen ich …
5  Closing, hope: Ich hoffe, dass …

cards.title: Utopia or dystopia?
cards.body: A vision can be bright, an Utopie, or dark, a Dystopie. Good speakers show both sides: hope and worry. Use Ich hoffe, dass … for hope and Ich habe Angst, dass … or Ich mache mir Sorgen, dass … for worry. In dass-clauses werden stands at the end. You can combine both with aber or trotzdem.
cards.lead: Not every picture of the future is happy. This last card gives you the phrases for fears and worries, so your visions can be honest and balanced, not only bright.

examples.de: Ich habe Angst, dass es in 20 Jahren zu heiß sein wird.
examples.en: I am afraid that it will be too hot in 20 years.

examples.de: Ich mache mir Sorgen, dass viele Menschen allein leben werden.
examples.en: I am worried that many people will live alone.

examples.de: Ich hoffe trotzdem, dass die Technik uns helfen wird.
examples.en: I still hope that technology will help us.

deeper.text: The word Utopie goes back to a book from 1516 by Thomas More, who named an imaginary island Utopia. The name comes from Greek and means no place. A Utopie is a place that does not exist. A Dystopie is its dark twin, an imagined future in which things have gone wrong. Today both words appear in newspapers, films and books about the future.

example.de: Eine Utopie ist ein Ort, den es nicht gibt.
example.en: A utopia is a place that does not exist.

cards.more: Think of a scale with two plates. On the left plate you put your hopes: Ich hoffe, dass … On the right plate you put your worries: Ich habe Angst, dass … A balanced speaker keeps both plates in view and says so with aber or trotzdem. Try it with one topic, for example the climate or technology. One sentence with hope, one with worry, and one with trotzdem. In three sentences you show that you think for yourself.

rows: Ich hoffe, dass wir mehr Zeit haben werden.
Ich mache mir Sorgen, dass es zu heiß wird.
Ich habe Angst, dass viele allein leben werden.
Ich hoffe trotzdem, dass die Technik uns hilft.

Ich würde gern in Wien wohnen.

drills.explanation: Von der Welt träume ich: von der.

prompts: Describe your vision of the world in 20 years in four sentences. Use one relative clause and one werden-sentence.
Say what you hope for and what worries you about the future. Use Ich hoffe, dass … and Ich mache mir Sorgen, dass …
Tell a friend one dream and one expectation. Use Es wäre schön, wenn … for the dream and Ich werde … for the expectation.
examples: Ich stelle mir eine Welt vor, in der alle genug Zeit haben. In 20 Jahren werden die Städte grüner sein. Die Menschen, mit denen ich lebe, helfen sich. Das ist meine Vision.
Ich hoffe, dass wir mehr Frieden haben werden. Aber ich mache mir Sorgen, dass es in 20 Jahren zu heiß sein wird.
Es wäre schön, wenn alle Menschen genug zu essen hätten. Ich werde in 20 Jahren wohl in einer anderen Stadt wohnen.

lessons.title: Was erwartest du? Erwartungen, und ss oder ß
lessons.goal: Talk about expectations and fears with dass and ob, and choose ß or ss by the length of the vowel.

grammar.topic: Expectations (use of dass, ob and Futur) and the spelling of ß and ss
grammar.point: No new grammar. Expectation openers (erwarten, rechnen damit, befürchten, gespannt sein ob) start a clause with the verb at the end; with Futur werden comes last. Spelling: long vowel or diphthong + ß, short vowel + ss.
grammar.oneLine: Ich erwarte, dass ich schnell Freunde finden werde.

mistake.wrong: Ich erwarte, dass ich werde schnell Freunde finden.
mistake.right: Ich erwarte, dass ich schnell Freunde finden werde.
mistake.why: In a dass-clause the conjugated verb goes to the end. With Futur that is werden, after the infinitive.

terms.meaning: what you think will happen, good or bad (die Erwartung)
two vowels said as one sound: ei, au, eu

cards.title: Before we start: from 'Ich hoffe, dass …' to 'Ich erwarte, dass …'
cards.body: Anna moves to Wien in March, and Mira has an offer from Datenhafen. Before a big change, people say what they expect and what they fear. You can already hope and plan. Today you name expectations, fears and suspense, and you learn when German writes ß and when ss.
steps: You already know: Ich hoffe, dass … and Ich rechne damit, dass … (B1 ch04).
New today: Ich befürchte, dass es schwer wird. Ich bin gespannt, ob ich Freunde finden werde.
By the end: you can talk about your expectations and fears, and you can choose ß or ss by listening to the vowel.

examples.de: Ich hoffe, dass es in Wien schön wird.
examples.en: I hope that it will be nice in Wien.
examples.why: You know this: hoffen + dass, verb at the end.

examples.de: Ich befürchte, dass es am Anfang schwer wird.
examples.en: I am afraid that it will be hard at the beginning.
examples.why: New: befürchten works exactly like hoffen.

examples.de: Ich bin gespannt, ob ich Freunde finden werde.
examples.en: I am curious whether I will find friends.
examples.why: New: gespannt + ob, Futur at the end.

cards.more: Picture Anna packing a suitcase for Wien. Into one pocket go her hopes, into another her fears, and into a third the questions she cannot answer yet. German has a fixed opener for each pocket: hoffen for hopes, befürchten for fears, gespannt sein for open questions. After each opener comes a comma and a clause with the verb at the end. So you are not learning new grammar today, only new openers for a sentence pattern you already use every day.

cards.title: Erwartungen an Wien und an Mira
cards.lead: First a real scene. Anna tells Ben what she expects from Wien, and Mira talks with her team leader about the time after the Bachelor. Listen for the openers.
cards.body: Two short talks. Anna is excited about Wien but also a little worried. Datenhafen would like Mira to stay after her Bachelor, and Mira expects flexible hours while she writes her Bachelorarbeit from April. Notice: every expectation is a main clause plus dass or ob, and the verb goes to the end.
steps: Ben: Was erwartest du von Wien?
Anna: Ich erwarte, dass ich viel Neues lernen werde. Aber ich befürchte, dass ich Berlin vermissen werde.
Der Teamleiter: Wir hoffen, dass du nach dem Bachelor bei uns bleiben wirst.
Mira: Ich erwarte, dass ich ab April flexible Arbeitszeiten habe. Dann schreibe ich meine Bachelorarbeit.

examples.de: Ich erwarte, dass ich viel Neues lernen werde.
examples.en: I expect that I will learn a lot of new things.

examples.de: Wir hoffen, dass du nach dem Bachelor bei uns bleiben wirst.
examples.en: We hope that you will stay with us after your Bachelor.

examples.de: Ich befürchte, dass ich Berlin vermissen werde.
examples.en: I am afraid that I will miss Berlin.

deeper.text: Watch the prepositions. The verb is erwarten von + dative: Was erwartest du von Wien? But the noun takes an + accusative: meine Erwartungen an Wien, die Erwartungen an Mira. English uses 'of' or 'from' for both, German splits them. In job talks you will hear the noun form a lot: Welche Erwartungen haben Sie an die Stelle?

example.de: Meine Erwartungen an die neue Stadt sind hoch.
example.en: My expectations of the new city are high.

cards.more: Think of the two talks as two directions. Anna looks from herself towards Wien: what will the city give me? The team at Datenhafen looks from the company towards Mira: what will she give us, and will she stay? Mira answers with her own condition, flexible hours. Expectations always go both ways, and German uses the same frame for each side: an opener like erwarten or hoffen, a comma, dass, and the verb at the very end.

cards.title: Fünf Wege, Erwartungen auszudrücken
cards.lead: You heard the openers in the scene. This card puts the five most useful ones side by side, so you can pick the right one for your own plans.
cards.body: Each pattern opens a clause. erwarten and rechnen mit are neutral, sich etwas erhoffen is positive, befürchten is negative, and gespannt sein asks an open question with ob. After all five the verb goes to the end; with Futur, werden comes last.

rows: Ich erwarte, dass die Arbeit interessant wird.
Ich rechne damit, dass es am Anfang viel Arbeit gibt.
Ich erhoffe mir von Wien neue Ideen.
Ich befürchte, dass die Wohnung teuer sein wird.
Ich bin gespannt, ob Ben jeden Monat kommen kann.

examples.de: Ich rechne damit, dass es am Anfang viel Arbeit gibt.
examples.en: I expect that there will be a lot of work at the beginning.

examples.de: Ich erhoffe mir von Wien neue Ideen.
examples.en: I hope to get new ideas from Wien.

examples.de: Ich bin gespannt, ob Ben jeden Monat kommen kann.
examples.en: I am curious whether Ben can come every month.

deeper.text: Do not mix up erwarten and warten. warten auf means to wait: Ich warte auf den Bus. erwarten means to expect, and it takes a direct object without a preposition: Ich erwarte dich um acht means I expect you at eight. Wir erwarten Gäste means we are expecting guests. One extra syllable, a very different meaning.

example.de: Wir erwarten dich um acht Uhr im Café.
example.en: We expect you at eight o'clock in the café.

cards.more: Sort the five patterns like the colours of a traffic light. Green is sich etwas erhoffen: you wish for something good. Yellow is erwarten and rechnen mit: you think something will happen, good or bad. Red is befürchten: you think something bad may happen. The question mark is gespannt sein, ob: you really do not know and you are curious. Choose the colour first, then the opener, then build the clause with the verb at the end as always.

cards.title: Von Vorfreude bis Angst
cards.lead: The patterns have different feelings. Now we line them up from very positive to very negative, so you can show exactly how you feel about the future.
cards.body: Put the openers on a line. Left is pure joy, right is fear. Most real plans sit in the middle: you hope and you expect, but you also fear a little. Use two openers in one text to sound natural: Ich freue mich auf Wien, aber ich befürchte, dass …
steps: ++ sich freuen auf + Akk: Ich freue mich auf Wien.
+ hoffen, dass …: Ich hoffe, dass alles klappt.
0 erwarten, dass …: Ich erwarte, dass es viel Arbeit gibt.
- befürchten, dass …: Ich befürchte, dass ich Heimweh haben werde.
-- Angst haben vor + Dat: Ich habe Angst vor dem ersten Tag.

examples.de: Ich freue mich schon auf Wien.
examples.en: I am already looking forward to Wien.

examples.de: Ich befürchte, dass ich Heimweh haben werde.
examples.en: I'm afraid I will be homesick.

examples.de: Ich habe Angst vor dem ersten Tag.
examples.en: I am afraid of the first day.

deeper.text: befürchten sounds softer and more polite than Angst haben. In emails and at work it often means 'I am afraid' in the polite English sense: Ich befürchte, dass ich am Freitag nicht kommen kann. Nobody is scared here, it is a kind way to give bad news. Angst haben is a real, strong feeling.

example.de: Ich befürchte, dass ich am Freitag nicht kommen kann.
example.en: I'm afraid I can't come on Friday.

cards.more: Imagine a thermometer for the future. At the top it is warm: you are looking forward and full of Vorfreude. Lower down you only hope. In the middle you calmly expect. Further down it gets cold: you fear, and at the bottom you are afraid. When you speak about a big change, move along the thermometer: start warm, name one cold point honestly, and end warm again. That is how Germans often talk about plans: optimistic, but not naive.

cards.title: Langer Vokal: ß – kurzer Vokal: ss
cards.lead: Now the second topic of today: sound and spelling. Expectations often use dass, muss and weiß. Here is how to hear whether a word needs ß or ss.
cards.body: Say the word and listen to the vowel before the s-sound. Long vowel: ß, as in Straße, Fuß, groß, Gruß, bloß. Short vowel: ss, as in Fluss, muss, wissen, Kuss, Masse. The pair Maße and Masse shows it: long a with ß, short a with ss.

examples.de: Die Straße ist sehr lang.
examples.en: The street is very long.
examples.why: Long a before ß: Straaaße.

examples.de: Der Fluss ist nicht groß.
examples.en: The river is not big.
examples.why: Short u in Fluss, long o in groß.

examples.de: Ich muss bloß noch einpacken.
examples.en: I only have to pack.
examples.why: Short u in muss, long o in bloß.

deeper.text: Before 1996 Germans wrote daß, muß and Fluß with ß even after a short vowel. The spelling reform of 1996 made the rule simple: short vowel, ss. That is why you still see daß in old books and on old signs. It is not wrong for its time, it is just the old spelling.

example.de: Früher schrieb man „daß“, heute schreibt man „dass“.
example.en: In the past people wrote „daß“, today people write „dass“.

cards.more: Think of ß as a long word and ss as a short word on paper. A long vowel is like stretching a rubber band: Straaaße, Fuuuß, grooooß. After a stretch comes the single, elegant ß. A short vowel is like a quick knock: Fluss, muss, Kuss. After a quick knock come two letters, ss, just like the double letters in Butter or kommen. So double letters after short vowels are the normal German pattern, and ss is simply one more example of it.

cards.title: Die Regel in drei Schritten
cards.lead: You can hear the difference now. This card turns it into a quick spelling test you can run in your head whenever you write an s-sound.
cards.body: Three checks: 1. Is there a diphthong before the s-sound (ei, au, eu)? Then always ß: heißen, draußen, weiß. 2. Is the vowel long? ß. 3. Is it short? ss. In Switzerland there is no ß at all: Swiss German writes Strasse and gross, and that is correct there.
steps: 1 Diphthong (ei, au, eu) before the s-sound → ß: heißen, draußen
2 Long vowel → ß: die Straße, der Gruß
3 Short vowel → ss: der Fluss, wissen
In Switzerland: always ss (die Strasse)

examples.de: Wie heißen Sie?
examples.en: What is your name?
examples.why: ei is a diphthong, so ß.

examples.de: Draußen ist es heute kalt.
examples.en: It is cold outside today.
examples.why: au is a diphthong, so ß.

examples.de: Ich weiß nicht, ob ich Heimweh haben werde.
examples.en: I don't know whether I will be homesick.
examples.why: ei in weiß, so ß.

deeper.text: There is also a capital ẞ. It has been an official letter since 2017, but you will see it rarely. Most signs written in capitals still use SS: STRASSE. So in capitals both are possible, and in normal writing with small letters you use the rule from this card.

example.de: Auf dem Schild steht „STRASSE“.
example.en: The sign says „STRASSE“.

cards.more: Picture a little guard in front of every s-sound. The guard asks three questions in order. First: is there a double vowel sound like ei or au in front of me? Then the door opens for ß. Second: is the vowel in front of me long? Again ß. Third: is it short? Then ss gets in. The guard never asks about meaning, only about sound. That is why a quick look in the mirror while you say the word is often the best spelling help.

cards.title: Ein Verb, zwei Schreibungen
cards.lead: The rule has a surprise: one verb can change between ss and ß. Because the vowel changes its length, the spelling changes with it, even inside one verb.
cards.body: wissen has a short i, so ss. But er weiß has the diphthong ei, so ß. essen has a short e: ich esse, er isst. The Präteritum aß has a long a, so ß. The spelling simply follows the sound in every form.

examples.de: Mira weiß noch nicht, ob sie bleibt.
examples.en: Mira doesn't know yet whether she will stay.

examples.de: Leon isst jeden Donnerstag im Kochkurs.
examples.en: Leon eats in his cooking course every Thursday.

examples.de: Gestern aß Anna zum letzten Mal bei Herrn Ali.
examples.en: Yesterday Anna ate at Herr Ali's for the last time.

deeper.text: The Präteritum of wissen is wusste, with a short u: ich wusste, er wusste, and the Perfekt is hat gewusst. So the verb goes ss, ß, ss: wir wissen, er weiß, er wusste. If you know the sound of each form, you will never need to learn these spellings by heart.

example.de: Ich wusste nicht, dass Anna nach Wien geht.
example.en: I didn't know that Anna is going to Wien.

cards.more: Imagine the verb wissen as a person who changes clothes for every occasion. At home with wir and ihr it wears the short ss. When er or sie speak, it puts on the long coat ß: er weiß. In the past it wears ss again: wusste, gewusst. The person stays the same, only the clothes change. The same is true for essen: isst today, aß yesterday. Read every form aloud, listen for the vowel, and you can dress the verb correctly yourself.

lessons.title: Ich kann es kaum erwarten: ein Lied
lessons.goal: Understand a short song, talk about it with song words and handeln von, use es kaum erwarten können, and learn German with music.

grammar.topic: A song (use of Futur, a relative clause with a preposition and the chunk es kaum erwarten können)
grammar.point: No new grammar. The chunk es kaum erwarten können works with es + zu + infinitive or with a noun in place of es. Talking about a song uses handeln von + dative and a relative clause (die Zeile, in der …).
grammar.oneLine: Ich kann es kaum erwarten, dich zu sehen.

mistake.wrong: Ich kann kaum erwarten, dich zu sehen.
mistake.right: Ich kann es kaum erwarten, dich zu sehen.
mistake.why: The chunk needs es: it points forward to the zu-part. Without a noun, es must be there.

terms.meaning: a group of words you learn together, like es kaum erwarten können
a catchy German pop song with a simple refrain

cards.title: Before we start: from 'Ich freue mich' to 'Ich kann es kaum erwarten'
cards.body: The WG is planning a farewell party for Anna, and Anna has written a short song for it. Songs are a great way to learn chunks, rhythm and pronunciation. You can already say that you look forward to something. Today you learn a stronger, more emotional way to say it, and you learn how to talk about a song.
steps: You already know: Ich freue mich auf Wien.
New today: Ich kann es kaum erwarten, dich wiederzusehen.
By the end: you can understand a short song, describe it with Strophe, Refrain and Reim, and use music to learn German.

examples.de: Ich freue mich auf die Party.
examples.en: I'm looking forward to the party.
examples.why: You know this: sich freuen auf + accusative.

examples.de: Ich kann es kaum erwarten.
examples.en: I can hardly wait.
examples.why: New: the chunk es kaum erwarten können.

examples.de: Ich kann es kaum erwarten, dich wiederzusehen.
examples.en: I can hardly wait to see you again.
examples.why: New: the chunk + zu + infinitive; wiedersehen has zu in the middle.

cards.more: Imagine two friends waiting for the same train. The first one says: Ich freue mich auf den Urlaub. She is calm and smiling. The second one keeps looking at the clock and walks up and down: Ich kann es kaum erwarten! Both are happy, but the second one is impatient in a good way. That is the difference you learn today. And because Anna puts her feelings into a song, you will also learn the words that people use to talk about music.

cards.title: Annas Lied: „Ich kann es kaum erwarten“
cards.lead: Here is Anna's song for the farewell party. Read it aloud slowly once, then look for every werde or wird and for the one relative clause.
cards.body: Two verses and a refrain that comes back. Verse 1 is about leaving Berlin, verse 2 about the year in Wien and coming home. The song uses Futur for promises, one relative clause with a preposition, and the chunk of today in the refrain.
steps: Strophe 1: Der Koffer steht im Flur, im März geht es los,
ein Jahr in Wien allein, die Freude ist so groß.
Ich werde euch vermissen, die Küche und den Tisch,
an dem wir abends saßen, mit Leons Pasta, frisch.
Refrain: Ich kann es kaum erwarten, ich kann es kaum erwarten,
in Wien wird bald ein neues Leben auf mich warten.
Strophe 2: Ben wird mich jeden Monat besuchen, mit dem Zug,
und ein Wochenende ist für uns nie genug.
Und wenn das Jahr zu Ende ist, sitzen wir hier zu viert,
und jeder wird erzählen, was in dem Jahr passiert.
Refrain: Ich kann es kaum erwarten, ich kann es kaum erwarten,
in Wien wird bald ein neues Leben auf mich warten.

examples.de: Ich werde euch vermissen.
examples.en: I will miss you (all).
examples.why: Futur: a promise and a feeling about the future.

examples.de: … den Tisch, an dem wir abends saßen.
examples.en: … the table at which we sat in the evenings.
examples.why: Relative clause with a preposition (lesson 8).

examples.de: In Wien wird bald ein neues Leben auf mich warten.
examples.en: In Wien a new life will soon be waiting for me.
examples.why: Futur with warten auf.

deeper.text: The refrain plays with two verbs you met in lesson 10: erwarten and warten. They look almost the same and they rhyme, but they mean different things. Ich kann es kaum erwarten is about Anna's impatience. Ein neues Leben wird auf mich warten is about the life that waits for her. Songs love such pairs.

example.de: Ich warte auf den Zug, aber ich erwarte keinen Platz.
example.en: I'm waiting for the train, but I don't expect a seat.

cards.more: Read the song like a little film in three scenes. Scene one: a suitcase in the hall and a full table with Leon's pasta, which Anna will miss. Scene two: a year in Wien, Ben on the train every month, weekends that are always too short. Scene three: the four friends at the table again, telling stories. Between the scenes the refrain comes back like a chorus in a film. Every scene uses German you know, only arranged with rhythm and rhyme.

cards.title: Wörter für Lieder
cards.lead: To talk about Anna's song you need a few words for the parts of a song. They work for every song you like, in any language.
cards.body: A song has Strophen (verses) and a Refrain (chorus) that comes back. Each Strophe has Zeilen (lines). Two lines often end with a Reim: Wien reimt sich auf hin, los auf groß. The Melodie is the tune, the Rhythmus is the beat. The words of a song are der Liedtext.

examples.de: Das Lied hat zwei Strophen.
examples.en: The song has two verses.

examples.de: „Los“ reimt sich auf „groß“.
examples.en: „Los“ rhymes with „groß“.

examples.de: Den Refrain singen alle mit.
examples.en: Everyone sings along with the chorus.

deeper.text: In songs German often drops the final -e of a verb: ich hab', ich geh', fahr' ich. Anna writes im März fahr' ich nach Wien. This is for the rhythm, and it is also normal in everyday speech. In formal writing, such as a letter to an office, you write the full form: ich habe, ich fahre.

example.de: Im März fahr' ich nach Wien.
example.en: In March I'm going to Wien.

cards.more: Think of a song as a small house. The Strophen are the rooms, each a bit different. The Refrain is the hall you walk through again and again between the rooms. The Zeilen are the bricks, and the Reime are the places where two bricks fit perfectly together. The Rhythmus is your step when you walk through the house, and the Melodie is the colour of the walls. With these six words you can describe any song.

cards.title: es kaum erwarten können
cards.lead: The refrain is built on one chunk. This card takes it apart, so you can use it for your own plans and not only in Anna's song.
cards.body: The chunk is es kaum erwarten können: to be hardly able to wait. Two patterns: with es + zu + infinitive (Ich kann es kaum erwarten, dich zu sehen) or with a noun instead of es (Ich kann den Sommer kaum erwarten). können is the conjugated verb, erwarten goes to the end.

rows: Ich kann es kaum erwarten, Wien zu sehen.
Leon kann den Kochkurs kaum erwarten.

examples.de: Ich kann es kaum erwarten, Wien zu sehen.
examples.en: I can hardly wait to see Wien.

examples.de: Leon kann den Kochkurs kaum erwarten.
examples.en: Leon can hardly wait for the cooking course.

examples.de: Wir können den Sommer kaum erwarten.
examples.en: We can hardly wait for the summer.

deeper.text: kaum means hardly, almost not: Ich habe kaum geschlafen. So the chunk literally says I can almost not wait, and that is why it means positive impatience. Do not replace kaum with nicht: Ich kann es nicht erwarten is not the normal phrase. The fixed chunk is always with kaum.

example.de: Ich habe heute kaum geschlafen.
example.en: I hardly slept today.

cards.more: Imagine a child on the evening before a birthday. The child cannot sit still, asks every five minutes how long it is, and looks at the presents again and again. That feeling is es kaum erwarten können. Adults use it for the same feeling: a holiday, a visit, a new job, a concert. The word es is a placeholder that points forward to the zu-part, so you either keep es and add zu + infinitive, or you put the thing directly in its place.

cards.title: Über ein Lied sprechen
cards.lead: Now you know the parts of a song and the chunk of the refrain. These sentences help you say what a song is about and why you like it.
cards.body: Four useful openers: Das Lied handelt von + dative (what it is about). Die Stimmung ist … (the mood). Mir gefällt die Zeile, in der … (a line you like). Der Refrain ist ein Ohrwurm (it stays in your head). With them you can give a short opinion on any song.

rows: Das Lied handelt von einem Abschied.
Die Stimmung ist traurig und froh zugleich.
Mir gefällt die Zeile, in der …
Mir gefällt die Zeile, in der Ben mit dem Zug kommt.
Ich summe ihn den ganzen Tag.

examples.de: Das Lied handelt von einem Abschied.
examples.en: The song is about a farewell.

examples.de: Mir gefällt die Zeile, in der Ben mit dem Zug kommt.
examples.en: I like the line in which Ben comes by train.

examples.de: Der Refrain ist ein Ohrwurm.
examples.en: The chorus is an earworm.

deeper.text: handeln von means to be about. Without von, handeln means to act or to trade: Wir müssen jetzt handeln (we must act now). On a market you can also handeln about the price. So von changes the meaning completely. For books, films and songs you always say: Es handelt von …

example.de: Der Film handelt von einer Familie in Wien.
example.en: The film is about a family in Wien.

cards.more: Think of these four openers as four questions a friend asks after you play a song. What is it about? Answer with handelt von. How does it feel? Answer with die Stimmung ist. Which part do you like best? Answer with mir gefällt die Zeile, in der. Does it stay with you? Answer with Ohrwurm. If you can answer all four, you have given a complete little review, and you have used a dative, a relative clause and a chunk.

cards.title: Deutsch lernen mit Musik
cards.lead: Songs are not only for parties. This card shows a simple five-step method to learn German with any song, like the Easy German video of this lesson.
cards.body: Songs repeat chunks, so you hear them many times without getting bored. The rhythm helps your pronunciation, and the melody helps your memory. Follow five steps with one song per week. The video of this lesson shows the same idea with real songs.
steps: 1 Listen to the song two or three times.
2 Read the Liedtext and look up a few words.
3 Sing along (mitsingen), quietly at first.
4 Learn one line by heart (auswendig).
5 Use one chunk from the song in your own sentence.

examples.de: Zuerst höre ich das Lied dreimal.
examples.en: First I listen to the song three times.

examples.de: Dann lese ich den Liedtext.
examples.en: Then I read the lyrics.

examples.de: Am Ende singe ich den Refrain mit.
examples.en: At the end I sing along with the chorus.

deeper.text: Ohrwurm is a German word: Ohr (ear) + Wurm (worm). English borrowed it as earworm, a tune you cannot get out of your head. For learners an Ohrwurm is a gift: if a German refrain is stuck in your head, you are practising the chunk all day without trying.

example.de: Der Refrain ist mein neuer Ohrwurm.
example.en: The chorus is my new earworm.

cards.more: Think of a song as a bus that takes you through the same street every day. The first time you only see colours. The second time you see the shops. After a week you know every sign by heart. Songs work like that bus: the same words come back again and again, always with the same melody, so your brain stores them almost by itself. Your job is only to get on the bus regularly and, at the end, to walk one street on your own.

cards.title: Singen in D-A-CH
cards.lead: Last, a look at culture. Where and how do people in Germany, Austria and Switzerland sing together, and what will you hear at a German party?
cards.body: Many people in D-A-CH sing along at parties, weddings and football games, often to Schlager (catchy German pop songs) and to German pop. Karaoke is popular too. Not everyone sings, of course, but if a famous refrain starts, many people know the words and join in.
steps: Party, Hochzeit, Fußball: people often sing along.
Schlager: catchy German songs with a simple refrain.
Karaoke: you sing to the music, the text is on a screen.
Tendency only: not everyone sings.

examples.de: Auf der Hochzeit singen viele mit.
examples.en: At the wedding many people sing along.

examples.de: Den Schlager kennt fast jeder.
examples.en: Almost everyone knows the Schlager.

examples.de: Beim Karaoke summe ich lieber.
examples.en: At karaoke I'd rather hum.

deeper.text: summen means to hum, singing with your mouth closed. It is a good first step if you are shy: summ the melody first, then add the words of the refrain. Many Germans summen when they do not know the text, so nobody will think it is strange at a party.

example.de: Wenn ich den Text nicht kenne, summe ich.
example.en: When I don't know the lyrics, I hum.

cards.more: Imagine Anna's farewell party in the WG kitchen. Leon puts music on, Herr Ali brings food, Frau Weber claps. When Anna plays her song a second time, the others already sing along with the refrain, Mira the loudest. Ben hums because he forgot the words. That is a typical scene: nobody has to sing well, the point is to be together. If you join in, even quietly, people will like it, and you will remember the refrain for a long time.
